lessons.plain: A project vision is a short, clear picture of what the project is meant to achieve and why it matters. A shared vision means the people working on it, and the people paying for or using it, all picture roughly the same outcome. Your job as project manager is to help build that picture, repeat it in plain words, and check that it still lives in people's heads. When different people start describing the goal differently, something upstream has gone wrong, and the job is to find the cause rather than just correct the wording.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two team members on the same project each describe its goal to you. One says 'a faster checkout page' and the other says 'fewer abandoned carts.' Before any teaching, what do you think might explain the gap between them, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A project vision is a concise statement of the outcome a project is meant to produce and the value it should create for the people it serves. A shared vision is one that the sponsor (the person funding and accountable for the project), the team, and key stakeholders have all heard, understood, and accepted in roughly the same terms. Promoting the vision means repeating it in plain language, linking daily tasks back to it, and inviting questions so people can test their understanding. Diagnosing divergence means finding out why people's descriptions of the goal differ. That is a different task from correcting their wording.

It works because people act on the picture they hold. If two engineers believe the goal is speed and two others believe it is fewer lost customers, each pair will make reasonable but conflicting trade-offs, and no one is wrong about their own task.

Worked example. A project to reduce delivery delays is described by the sponsor as 'on-time arrivals for customers.' Step one: collect each person's own wording without correcting it. Step two: note where the wording differs. The warehouse reads 'on-time' as 'shipped on time,' while drivers read it as 'arrived within the delivery window.' Step three: trace the source. The original business case used shipping dates, and the sponsor's kickoff slide was edited later to say arrival. Step four: restate the vision with a measurable definition, confirm it with the sponsor, and walk the team through the change.

A common mistake is to restate the vision more loudly and assume the gap has closed. Repetition does not fix a vision that was never agreed, or one that changed in one document but not in the others.

When divergence goes undiagnosed, teams build against different targets, and the mismatch surfaces late as rework or rejected deliverables. Finding the root cause early is cheaper than correcting the output later.

questions.prompt: A city council project aims to cut library book-return backlogs. The sponsor (the official funding the project and accountable for its result) describes the goal as 'books back on the shelves quickly.' Four staff members give their own wording without correction. The circulation desk says 'every return checked in within one working day.' The shelving team says 'returned items reshelved within two days.' The branch managers say 'no overdue fines from late check-in.' Step one, collecting each person's wording without correcting it, is done. Step two, noting where the wording differs, is done: the three groups disagree on both the start point and the end point. Step three, tracing the source, is done: the original grant proposal measured 'days from return to reshelving,' but the sponsor's kickoff slide was later changed to say 'checked in.' Step four is missing. What should the project lead do next?
choices: Repeat the sponsor's kickoff slide wording at every team meeting until the three groups converge
Stop the backlog work until each group has written a separate project vision for its own area
Restate the vision with one measurable definition, confirm it with the sponsor, then walk all three groups through the change
Ask the shelving team to drop its own target so that everyone works to the circulation desk's definition
questions.why: After the root cause is found, the fix is to restate the vision in measurable terms, get the sponsor to agree, and then explain the change to the team, because only an agreed and communicated definition closes the gap.

questions.prompt: In this teaching text, what does it mean for a project vision to be shared?
choices: Each group has its own version of the vision that fits its own tasks
The vision is printed on every project document and filed in the shared drive
The sponsor, the team, and key stakeholders have all heard, understood, and accepted it in roughly the same terms
The team has voted to adopt the vision and the sponsor has signed a copy of it
questions.why: The text defines a shared vision as one that the sponsor, team, and key stakeholders have heard, understood, and accepted in roughly the same terms, not one that is merely written down or voted on.

questions.prompt: A logistics team is building a route-planning tool. Two developers describe the project goal differently: one says it is about cutting fuel costs, the other says it is about fewer missed pickups. The project manager wants to find out why their descriptions differ. Which first action fits the diagnosis step described in the teaching text?
choices: Ask each developer to describe the goal in their own words and note where the wording differs, without correcting it
Choose the description that matches the business case and tell the other developer to follow it
Correct the developer who described the goal as fuel costs so both use the same wording
Schedule a training session on the project vision for the whole development team
questions.why: Diagnosing divergence starts by collecting each person's own wording without correcting it, and then noting where the wording differs, so the cause can be traced rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: A sponsor of a hospital equipment-sterilisation project repeats the vision 'safer instruments for surgery' in every meeting for six weeks. The team still builds tools against different targets, and rework is rising. What is the most likely reason repetition has not helped?
choices: The team members need a separate training course on what safety means in surgery
The vision was never actually agreed, or its source documents still differ, so repeating the same words cannot close the gap
The project has been running too long for a single vision statement to remain useful
The sponsor is not speaking loudly enough, so the team is not hearing the message
questions.why: The teaching text warns that repetition does not fix a vision that was never agreed, or one that changed in one document but not in the others, so the root cause must be found rather than the message repeated.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project how you would find out why the team's understanding of the project vision has split, and name one limit of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking each person, one to one, to describe the goal in their own words, and I would write down their exact phrases rather than correct them. That shows where the meanings split. Then I would look for the source: an older document, a sponsor's comment, a metric someone is measured on, or a term that means different things in different departments. Once I know the cause, I restate the vision with a definition everyone can test, confirm it with the sponsor, and check understanding again a week later. The limit is that this takes time and depends on people being candid. If people feel judged for not understanding, they may agree in the meeting and drift apart afterwards, so the check should ask what people would actually do, not just whether they agree.
rubricPoints: Gather each person's own wording before correcting anything.
Trace the divergence to its root cause, such as conflicting source documents or differing measures.
Restate the vision in a testable form and confirm it with the sponsor.
Name a limit, such as time cost or candour, and say how to check understanding afterwards.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a split vision from a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers team vision directly.

lessons.plain: Conflict is any clash between people on a project, whether over goals, facts, shared resources, or how work should be done. Managing it well means finding where the clash really starts, looking at the situation around it, choosing a response that fits, and agreeing on simple rules so it does not keep coming back. It is not the same as making the disagreement disappear or letting the loudest person win. A project manager's job is to keep disagreement productive while protecting the work and the people doing it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two team members keep arguing in standups about who owns a shared test environment. What would you check first before deciding what to do, and why?
lessons.teach: Conflict is a disagreement between people or groups whose goals, facts, or working habits clash, and it is normal on any project. Managing it means finding where the friction starts, understanding the surrounding situation, choosing a response on purpose, and then setting ground rules so the same friction does not return. The source is often not the loud argument itself. It might be a shortage of a shared resource, unclear roles, different priorities from different managers, or a personality clash that has been building for weeks. Analyzing context means asking what is at stake, how much time remains, how important the relationship is for future work, and whether the issue can be settled quickly. From there a project manager picks a strategy: collaborating to find an option everyone can support, compromising when both sides can give something, accommodating when the issue matters more to the other party, avoiding when the issue is trivial or will settle itself, or forcing a decision when a deadline or safety concern leaves no time. Each strategy fits some situations and harms others. Worked example: two developers disagree about whether a release should include a risky feature. The manager first confirms the source is the feature's testing deadline, not personal dislike. Context shows the release date is fixed and the test team is overloaded. The manager chooses collaboration, meets both developers with the test data, and asks them to propose a reduced scope. They agree, and the manager records the decision and its owner. Common mistake: resolving the argument of the day without fixing the cause, so the same dispute returns next sprint. Ground rules, such as named decision owners and a rule that disagreements are raised within one day, prevent that. Consequence: unresolved conflict quietly slows delivery and pushes good people away from the team, so the cause must be addressed as well as the symptom.

questions.prompt: Ana manages a warehouse with two shift leads, Ravi and Dee, who both need the single forklift from 6am to 10am. Ravi says Dee keeps booking it early. Ana checks the booking log and finds the forklift is double-booked because the sheet has no time slots. Context: peak season starts in 9 days, both leads are valuable to keep, and no spare forklift can be rented this week. Ana chooses collaboration, sits both leads down with the log, and they agree to split the morning into two timed slots. Ana writes the agreed slots down and names herself as the owner of any change. What step is still missing before the team can be confident this dispute will not return?
choices: Set a ground rule, such as timed slots kept in one shared place and a rule that clashes are raised within one day.
Give the forklift to Ravi for the whole of peak season.
Stop using the forklift until the peak season has ended.
Ask Dee to apologize to Ravi in front of the whole shift.
questions.why: Ground rules that prevent recurrence, such as shared timed booking and a one-day escalation rule, are the step that addresses the cause after the immediate dispute is settled.

questions.prompt: A project manager sees two team members arguing loudly during a daily stand-up. Before choosing a response, what should she establish first?
choices: Which person is right, so the argument can end quickly.
Whether the stand-up can be moved to another room.
Whether the friction comes from a resource shortage, unclear roles, conflicting priorities, or a clash that has built up over time.
How many minutes remain in the stand-up.
questions.why: The source of the conflict must be identified before a strategy is chosen, and the loud argument is often only a visible symptom of a deeper cause.

questions.prompt: A manager settles a dispute between two suppliers about invoice timing by giving each supplier the outcome it asked for, then closes the file without finding out why the dispute began. A month later the same dispute is back. Which mistake most likely caused this?
choices: Writing ground rules before meeting the suppliers.
Choosing forcing when the issue was not urgent.
Resolving the argument of the day without addressing the underlying cause, so the dispute returns.
Using accommodation when the supplier relationship was unimportant.
questions.why: Settling only the visible argument leaves the cause in place, so the same dispute reappears later, which is the common mistake this topic warns about.

questions.prompt: Two designers on a five-person team disagree about a button colour. The choice affects neither users, scope, nor the launch date, and both designers agree the colour can be revisited after launch without cost. Which strategy fits best?
choices: Forcing a decision now, because any disagreement threatens the launch.
Compromising by giving each designer half of the button to design.
Accommodating one designer's choice permanently to keep the peace.
Avoiding the disagreement for now, because the issue is trivial and will be settled later without harm.
questions.why: Avoiding is the right strategy when the issue is trivial or will settle itself, and here neither outcome changes anything important before launch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would handle a recurring argument between two engineers. Cover how you would find the real source, which resolution strategy you would choose and its main limit, and which ground rule you would set so the argument does not come back.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by separating the stated argument from its source. If two engineers keep fighting about a shared environment, the real cause is often unclear ownership or a scheduling clash, so I would ask each of them and the people who depend on the environment what actually goes wrong. Next I would look at context: how urgent the environment is, how long the disagreement has run, and whether the two of them must keep working together. For this I would probably choose collaboration, bringing them together to agree on a usage schedule, because it gets a solution both can support. Its limit is that it takes time and can stall if one person will not engage, in which case I would escalate to a decision. Finally I would set a ground rule: each shared resource gets a named owner, and disputes go to that owner within a day. That stops the same fight from restarting.
rubricPoints: Identifies the underlying source of the conflict rather than just the visible argument
Analyzes context such as urgency, history, and the need for an ongoing working relationship
Names a specific resolution strategy and explains its tradeoff or limit
Describes a ground rule that prevents recurrence

suggested.rationale: Handling conflict depends on reasoning through a situation and explaining the chosen response, which is not practiced by any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Leading a project team means guiding a group of people toward shared work without doing all the work yourself. In practice that covers four jobs: agreeing on how the team will work together, letting people make decisions that fit their role, helping them untangle problems instead of solving each one for them, and carrying the team's concerns to people above or outside the team. A leader also chooses how hands-on to be. A new team that does not know the domain may need clear direction, while a seasoned team may need only support and room to decide. The skill is matching the approach to the team in front of you, and then adjusting as the team grows.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of experienced engineers keeps missing its own deadlines and says the plan is unrealistic. Would you tell them exactly what to do, ask what they need, or do both? Why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A working agreement is a short, written set of rules the team makes for itself, such as when people respond to messages, how blockers get flagged, and what done means. Decision rights are the choices a team member may make alone, within limits the leader sets. Situational leadership is the idea that the right style depends on the team's readiness, meaning its skill and its willingness on the task at hand, so the leader moves between directing, coaching, supporting and delegating.

Why it works: people commit to rules they helped write, and they act faster when they know which decisions are theirs. A leader who sets the boundaries and then steps back usually gets more reliable results than one who checks every choice.

Worked example: a five-person team, two members new to the tooling, due in three weeks. Step 1: the leader runs a session where the team drafts a working agreement covering blocker flags and the definition of done. Step 2: for the tooling, the leader directs closely in week one, pairing newcomers with experienced members. Step 3: as skills grow, the leader shifts to coaching and gives the team authority to choose its test approach within the budget. Step 4: when a vendor dependency stalls, the leader asks the team for options before picking one. Step 5: when the team says the date is unrealistic, the leader takes their data to the sponsor rather than passing the pressure back down.

Common mistake: treating one style as a fixed personality trait and applying it everywhere, or handing over authority without the guardrails that make it safe.

Consequence: a team that waits for approval on every choice falls behind, while a team left without direction drifts from the plan.

Leadership means matching the approach to the team's readiness while staying accountable for the outcome.

questions.prompt: A nine-person customer support team at a regional insurer is moving to a new ticketing system, and one agent has never used it. Go-live is in four weeks. Step 1: the team leader runs a short session where the team writes its own working agreement covering how blockers are flagged and what counts as a resolved ticket. Step 2: for the first week the leader directs closely, with the new agent shadowing a senior agent. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: when the vendor's customer data import stalls, the leader asks the team for two or three workarounds before choosing one. The step 3 the leader takes is the one that fits this situation: the new agent now handles routine tickets alone, and the team is ready to own its routing rules. Which step 3 fits?
choices: Keep directing every routing decision so nothing slips before go-live.
Hand over every decision, including the go-live date, with no stated limits so the team is fully autonomous.
Move to coaching, and give the team authority to set its routing rules within a limit the leader states in advance.
Take the team's readiness data to the vendor and postpone the routing change.
questions.why: Rising readiness calls for a shift from directing to coaching, and handing authority over is safe only when the leader sets the boundaries first.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a working agreement?
choices: A list of job titles and reporting lines drawn up by human resources.
A short written set of rules the team makes for itself, such as response times and what done means.
A log of every risk the team has identified, with an owner for each risk.
A contract the leader signs with the sponsor that fixes the project budget.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a working agreement as a short, written set of rules the team creates for itself, and the other options describe different project documents.

questions.prompt: A leader uses the same directive style with a team of experienced members who already know the tools and the task. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The team waits for approval on routine choices and falls behind the plan.
The team writes a stronger working agreement because the leader sets all the rules.
The sponsor is more likely to approve a later date because the leader is in control.
The team gains skill faster because the leader is checking every step.
questions.why: The teaching text says a team that waits for approval on every choice falls behind, and treating one style as fixed ignores the team's readiness.

questions.prompt: Mid-project, the team tells the leader the delivery date is unrealistic, backed by their estimates. What should the leader do?
choices: Ask the team to drop the testing work to protect the date.
Tell the team to work longer hours so the date holds.
Wait until the date is missed, then ask the team why it slipped.
Take the team's data to the sponsor instead of passing the pressure back down to the team.
questions.why: The teaching text says the leader takes the team's data to the sponsor rather than passing the pressure back down, which keeps the leader accountable for the outcome.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a leadership style for a newly formed project team, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by judging the team's readiness on this specific task, not on general seniority. If members are new to the tools or the domain, I would give clear direction and pair people up, because guessing wastes time they do not have. As they show skill and confidence, I would move toward coaching and then delegation, giving them decision rights with defined limits. I would also set up a working agreement with them so expectations are shared and visible. The limit is that this takes ongoing attention: readiness differs by task and by person, so I have to re-check it regularly. If I move too fast, the team stalls; if I stay directive too long, they stop growing and I become a bottleneck.
rubricPoints: Chooses a style based on the team's readiness for the specific task, not a fixed personality
Explains how expectations are set through a shared working agreement
Describes giving decision rights with clear limits to empower the team
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as the need to reassess readiness or the risk of becoming a bottleneck

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying a leadership style is best practiced by explaining the reasoning aloud, and no listed mission or planned engine covers people-leadership skills.

lessons.plain: Stakeholders are the people or groups who can affect a project or be affected by it, such as sponsors, end users, regulators, and the teams that will support the result. Stakeholder engagement means finding them, understanding what each one cares about and how much influence they have, and then planning how to keep each one informed and involved in a way that suits them. Instead of sending everyone the same update, you choose the message, channel, and timing for each person, and you check whether the approach is working.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project sponsor has a lot of power over your budget but only hears from the project once a quarter, and she is about to be surprised by a delay. Before any teaching, what would you change about how you communicate with her, and why do you think that change would help?
lessons.teach:
Stakeholder engagement is the work of identifying stakeholders, analyzing them, and running a plan that brings each one to the right level of involvement. Identifying means listing everyone who can affect the project or be affected by it, including people outside the team. Analyzing means estimating, for each person, their influence (power to change outcomes), their interest (how much the outcome matters to them), their current engagement level (for example unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, or leading), and the level the project needs from them. The gap between current and needed engagement tells you what to do. Planning means deciding, for each stakeholder, what information they need, how often, through which channel, and which team member owns the relationship. A stakeholder engagement plan writes these decisions down so they can be reviewed and changed.

Why it works: people support what they understand and what they were consulted on. A high-influence stakeholder who hears bad news early can help solve it. The same person hearing it late tends to block it.

Worked example: a sponsor has high power and high interest but is only supportive, not leading. Step one, identify: she is on the list. Step two, analyze: current level supportive, needed level leading, because she must approve a scope change. Step three, plan: a short fortnightly one-to-one with a one-page summary of risks and pending decisions, plus a formal decision request before the next change review. At the next review, the change is approved.

Common mistake: sending all stakeholders the same weekly status email. This leaves powerful people under-informed and affected users without the detail they need.

Consequence: in a live programme, a stakeholder who learns about a cutover from a rumour may withhold access, and the release slips. The gap between where a stakeholder stands and where the project needs them is exactly what the engagement plan exists to close.

questions.prompt: A regional food distributor is replacing its dispatch software. Step one, identify: the list includes Mei, the head of cold-chain compliance. She can halt shipments, so she has high influence, and the outcome matters to her, so she has high interest. Step two, analyze: her current engagement is neutral, but the project needs her to be leading, because she must sign off a new temperature-logging change before go-live. The gap is between neutral and leading. Missing step, step three, plan: state the engagement action the planner should write down for Mei, including frequency, channel and owner.
choices: Remove her from the list because she is not yet supportive.
Send her the same weekly status email that every other stakeholder receives.
Hold a short fortnightly one-to-one with her, give her a one-page summary of open risks, and log a formal sign-off request before the logging review, owned by the project manager.
Tell her about the go-live date only in the final week, since she is neutral and busy.
questions.why: The planning step decides information, frequency, channel and owner for each stakeholder, and the option that sets all four to close the neutral-to-leading gap is the only one that does this.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm is moving its client billing to a new portal. Which person should be on the stakeholder list when the team first identifies stakeholders?
choices: Only the project team members who will build the portal.
Only people who have already complained about the project.
A client's finance clerk who will have to change how they pay invoices, even though they work outside the firm.
Only the firm's partners, since they hold the budget.
questions.why: Identifying means listing everyone who can affect the project or be affected by it, including people outside the team, so an external client's clerk who is affected belongs on the list.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team sends the same weekly status email to its executive sponsor, its night-shift supervisors and its vendor. Which outcome best matches the known failure of this approach?
choices: The sponsor, who has high power, is under-informed, and the supervisors who are affected lack the detail they need.
Nothing changes, because one message to everyone is the recommended approach.
The email is too frequent for everyone, so the sponsor stops reading project updates entirely.
The vendor gets too much detail and stops working on the project.
questions.why: Sending everyone the same message leaves powerful people under-informed and affected users without the detail they need, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A council IT project has a stakeholder rated high in influence, low in interest, and currently unaware of the project, while the project needs them to be supportive. What does the gap between current and needed engagement tell the planner?
choices: That the planner must choose engagement actions to move the stakeholder from unaware toward supportive, because the gap is what the engagement plan exists to close.
That the stakeholder's current level is already acceptable and no action is needed.
That the stakeholder should be dropped, since low interest means they cannot affect outcomes.
That the stakeholder's influence rating must be lowered to match their awareness.
questions.why: The gap between current and needed engagement tells the planner what to do, and the engagement plan exists to close that gap, so the correct choice is to plan actions to move the stakeholder toward supportive.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would identify and analyze the stakeholders on a new project, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing everyone who can affect the project or be affected by it, including people outside the team such as finance, regulators, end users, and the operations group that will support the result. For each person I would note their influence, their interest, where they currently stand in terms of support, and where we need them to be. That gap tells me what engagement is required. A high-influence person who is only neutral might need a short personal briefing, while an affected user group might need training and a demo. I would record these decisions in an engagement plan with a channel, frequency, and owner for each stakeholder. The main limit is that the analysis is only as good as our knowledge. Influence and attitude shift as the project moves, so the list and plan need reviewing at each phase, and quiet stakeholders are easy to underrate.
rubricPoints: Identify stakeholders broadly, including people outside the immediate team
Analyze each one for influence, interest, and current versus needed engagement level
Tailor channel, frequency, and owner to each stakeholder in an engagement plan
Name a real limit, such as stakeholder attitudes changing over time or incomplete knowledge

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying an engagement approach in a messy stakeholder situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no current or planned OpsForge mission or engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Stakeholders are anyone who can affect a project or be affected by it: sponsors who fund it, customers who use it, team members, suppliers, regulators, and the people who will run the result afterward. Managing their expectations means working out what each one believes the project will deliver, when, and at what cost, then bringing those beliefs into line with what the team can really do. Expectations drift quietly when nobody checks, so the job includes sorting people by how much power and interest they have, bringing disagreeing groups into one conversation, and watching whether customers are actually satisfied while the work progresses.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says the project must be finished by June, while a dispatch manager expects a scheduling screen that the team has never agreed to build. Before reading further, what would you do first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is any person or group with a stake in the project's outcome. Categorizing stakeholders means sorting them so you know how much attention each one needs. A common method is the power-interest grid. Power is how much influence a person has over decisions or funding. Interest is how much they care about the outcome. High power and high interest means manage closely. High power and low interest means keep satisfied. Low power and high interest means keep informed. Low power and low interest means monitor. Alignment is the state where stakeholders share the same written understanding of scope, timing, and quality. A facilitated alignment discussion gets the parties with conflicting expectations into one conversation, records each stated expectation, finds the overlap, and names the gaps. Customer satisfaction is measured against agreed acceptance criteria, not against how pleased people sound. Internal customers are other departments that use the output, and external customers are outside clients.

Worked example: a transit authority project has a sponsor who is high power and high interest and expects a June launch. A dispatch manager is high interest and medium power and wants a scheduling screen. A city regulator is high power and low interest and needs an audit trail. Step one, list all three and place them on the grid. Step two, hold one meeting with the sponsor and dispatch manager together. Step three, record that the June date excludes the screen unless another feature is traded out. Step four, get the agreed trade in writing. Step five, schedule a satisfaction check with dispatchers after each iteration.

The common mistake is treating all stakeholders alike or assuming silence means agreement. The consequence in a running system is that a quiet stakeholder rejects the output late, which forces rework and erodes trust in the schedule.

Alignment is kept current by repeating the check, not by holding it once at the start.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital is adding an appointment reminder system to its outpatient clinic. Stakeholders: the clinic director has high power and high interest; the billing office uses the output, has little power over the budget, and cares a lot about no-show fees; a state health inspector has high power over approval but low interest in day-to-day scheduling. Step one: place all three on the power-interest grid. The director goes in manage closely, the billing office goes in keep informed, and the inspector goes in keep satisfied. Step two: hold one facilitated alignment discussion with the director and the billing office in the same room. Step three is missing from this trace. Step four: get the agreed trade-off in writing. Which action belongs in step three?
choices: Let the director set the deadline and close the meeting
Record each stated expectation and name the overlap and gaps
Repeat the alignment check only once, at the kickoff meeting
Assume the inspector's silence means agreement and skip them
questions.why: A facilitated alignment discussion records each stated expectation, finds the overlap, and names the gaps before any trade-off is written down, so step three must be that recording and naming.

questions.prompt: A county water utility has a retired engineer on a community advisory panel. He has little say over funding decisions but follows every pipe replacement closely and writes to the board about it. Under the power-interest grid, which category fits him and what does that category call for?
choices: High power, low interest: keep satisfied
Low power, high interest: keep informed
High power, high interest: manage closely
Low power, low interest: monitor
questions.why: He has low power because he cannot influence funding, and high interest because he cares deeply, which the grid places in keep informed.

questions.prompt: On a software project, a vendor's project lead rarely speaks in weekly meetings, so the delivery team assumes the vendor accepts the revised scope. What is the best correction according to the alignment approach?
choices: Treat the silence as agreement, log it as aligned, and move on
Wait until final handover, when any disagreement will show itself
Run an alignment discussion and record the vendor's stated expectations in writing
Send the vendor a satisfaction survey after handover is complete
questions.why: Silence is not agreement, so the correct response is to bring the vendor into a facilitated discussion where each expectation is recorded and compared with the others.

questions.prompt: A small firm reports customer satisfaction as high because clients sounded pleased on recent calls. Which basis for measuring satisfaction does the approach in this course require?
choices: Count the positive emails received during the quarter
Rate it by how fast the support team answered tickets
Ask the sales lead how the calls sounded overall
Check the delivered output against the agreed acceptance criteria
questions.why: Customer satisfaction is measured against agreed acceptance criteria rather than how pleased people sound, so the delivered output must be checked against those criteria.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide how much attention each stakeholder gets, and how you would bring two stakeholders with conflicting expectations to one shared agreement. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by listing every stakeholder and placing each one on a power and interest grid, so the people with high power and high interest get the closest management, while low-power, low-interest people get periodic monitoring. For two stakeholders with conflicting expectations, I bring them into one facilitated conversation, have each state their expectation in writing, find the overlap, and name the specific gap, such as a date that cannot include a requested feature. We then agree a trade-off and record it. The main limit is that the grid is a snapshot: power and interest shift as the project moves, so I have to re-sort the stakeholders at each milestone. Another tradeoff is that bringing everyone together can take time that the team does not have, so I sometimes meet the two parties separately first.
rubricPoints: Stakeholders are categorized by power and interest, with a clear level of engagement for each category.
Conflicting expectations are brought into one facilitated discussion and recorded as an agreed baseline.
Customer satisfaction is checked against agreed acceptance criteria at regular points.
A limit or tradeoff is named, such as stakeholder positions changing over time or the time cost of alignment meetings.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission practices stakeholder categorization or alignment, so reasoning through an exam-style stakeholder scenario adds the most value here.

lessons.plain: Knowledge transfer means making sure what one person knows about a project does not stay locked in their head. On a project, people learn things that matter: why a vendor was chosen, a workaround that stops a crash, or which customer always asks for changes late. If that knowledge leaves when someone changes jobs or goes on holiday, the project pays to learn it again. This objective is about two jobs for the project manager: collecting that knowledge while the work runs and at its end, and setting up habits so people share it routinely instead of keeping it in silos.
lessons.guessPrompt: A senior engineer who knows how the billing system really works will leave the project in two weeks. What would you do first, and why might that matter more than the next sprint's tasks?
lessons.teach:
Tacit knowledge is know-how that people carry in their heads, such as judgment, workarounds, and the reasons behind a decision. Explicit knowledge is knowledge that has been written down or stored where others can find it. A knowledge silo is knowledge held by one person or group that others cannot easily reach. A lessons learned register is a running project record of what worked, what did not, and what to do differently, updated during the work rather than only at the end. Knowledge management is the set of practices for capturing, storing, and reusing this knowledge.

It works because knowledge is cheap to capture while the person who holds it is still on the project, and expensive or impossible to rebuild after they leave. Sharing also spreads the risk: when two people understand a component, one absence does not stop the work.

Worked example. Step 1: at each sprint review, the team adds one line to the lessons learned register, such as the map tile cache expires at 02:00 and breaks the morning dispatch view. Step 2: the billing engineer pairs with a second engineer for one afternoon and the session is recorded as a short written walkthrough. Step 3: both items are stored in the team's shared space and each has a named owner. Step 4: when the billing engineer leaves, a newcomer resolves a billing ticket from the walkthrough without interrupting the person who has gone.

Common mistake: treating knowledge transfer as one handover document written in the final week. By then the tacit knowledge has usually already been lost, and the document captures only what the person remembers under pressure.

In a running system the consequence is concrete. An undocumented workaround looks like an arbitrary setting until it fails during an outage months later, and nobody on the team knows why it exists or whether it is safe to change.

Knowledge that is shared as the work happens is the knowledge the project can still use after people move on.

questions.prompt: A freight firm's routing team wants its early-route knowledge kept after staff move on. Step 1: each Friday, the dispatcher adds one line to the lessons learned register, such as 'the depot gate code changes on the first Monday of the month, and the early-route file fails if it is not updated.' Step 2: the senior router pairs with a junior router for two hours, and the session is captured as a short recorded walkthrough. Step 3 is missing and must be filled in. Step 4: when the senior router moves to another depot, the junior router reruns the early-route file from the walkthrough without calling the person who has left.
choices: Store both the register line and the walkthrough in the team's shared space, with a named owner for each item.
Delete the Friday register lines once the walkthrough exists, so that the record stays short.
Keep the walkthrough in the senior router's personal folder so that access is restricted and errors are avoided.
Hold the full knowledge transfer as one handover document written in the final week before the senior router leaves.
questions.why: Storing both items in a shared space with a named owner is what makes them findable and maintained, which Step 4 depends on.

questions.prompt: A forecasting analyst on a retail project is the only person who knows why a safety-stock multiplier was set to 1.4 rather than 1.2, and that reason is written down nowhere. Which term best describes the reason itself?
choices: Explicit knowledge, because it is a setting stored in the configuration file.
A knowledge silo, because only one person holds it.
Tacit knowledge, because it is judgment carried in the analyst's head.
A lessons learned register entry, because it describes what worked.
questions.why: The reason behind a decision that lives only in someone's head is tacit knowledge, while the silo is the situation of it being unreachable, not the kind of knowledge itself.

questions.prompt: A team's lessons learned register on a nine-month contract is updated only in the final week. Which assessment is most accurate?
choices: The register should be deleted to avoid clutter, because a final summary is enough for the next project.
Too late if only at the end; update during the work.
Nothing is wrong, since end-of-project records are the usual standard in most organisations and they capture what matters.
The register should be shared only with the sponsor, so the team is not overloaded with notes during the work.
questions.why: Updating only at the end misses knowledge lost during the work, so the register should be kept current as the project runs.

questions.prompt: A payroll system's nightly batch needs a manual restart step that only one operator knows. Which action best supports knowledge transfer?
choices: Leave the restart step with the operator and record it in their annual review so they remain responsible for it.
Write the restart procedure in the final week before the operator's leave date, so it is ready for the handover.
Pair a second operator with the one who knows the step for a session, and store the recorded walkthrough with a named owner.
Ask the operator to answer questions by phone whenever a batch fails, so the knowledge stays available.
questions.why: Pairing a second person and storing the recorded walkthrough with a named owner shares the knowledge while the holder is still present and keeps it reachable after they leave.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would stop critical project knowledge from living in one person's head, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would make capture part of normal work rather than a final task. Each sprint review adds lessons to a shared register with an owner, and key experts pair with a second person so the knowledge gets written down while they are still around. Shared notes go in one searchable place the whole team uses. The main limit is time: pairing and documentation slow the people involved, and a project under deadline pressure tends to skip them first. So I would protect a small, fixed amount of time per sprint and check at reviews whether the register is actually being used. Another limit is that some knowledge, like judgment built from years of experience, cannot be fully written down, so pairing matters as much as documents.
rubricPoints: Captures knowledge during the work, not only in a final handover
Distinguishes knowledge that can be documented from tacit knowledge that needs pairing or conversation
Makes sharing routine with owners, a shared store, and regular checks
Names a real tradeoff such as time cost or the limits of what documents can capture

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is articulating how to capture and share knowledge, which no current mission or planned engine directly tests.

lessons.plain: Project communication is the planned way information moves between the people who do the work and the people who need to know about it. A communication strategy is a written plan that answers who needs what information, how often, in what form, and who is responsible for sending it. Feedback loops are the routes by which listeners reply, so the team can tell whether the message landed and correct course. Reports are the summaries that show progress to sponsors and stakeholders at the level of detail each one actually wants. Think of it like a transit timetable: it is only useful if it matches what each rider needs and someone checks whether the trains actually arrive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor tells you she hears about problems only after they are already late, but she does not want a flood of daily emails. What would you change first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A communication strategy is the plan that sets out, for a project, which stakeholders need which information, how often, in what format, through which channel, and who owns each message. A stakeholder is anyone who can affect the project or be affected by it. The sponsor is the person who funds the project and holds final authority over its goals. A good strategy starts from each stakeholder's needs, not from the habits of the team. A feedback loop is a deliberate route for the audience to reply, so the project learns whether a message was understood and whether the information is still useful. Communication takes three shapes: push (sent to recipients, such as a status summary), pull (made available for people to fetch, such as a shared dashboard), and interactive (a two-way discussion, such as a review meeting). It works because matching shape, frequency and detail to each audience keeps information flowing without overwhelming anyone, and feedback loops catch misunderstandings while they are still cheap to fix.

Worked example: the sponsor wants early warning on schedule risk. Step 1: record her need, which is risks that could move a milestone, flagged within one week. Step 2: pick a format, a one-page summary rating each milestone red, amber or green. Step 3: pick a frequency, every two weeks, plus an immediate call for any red item. Step 4: add a feedback loop by asking her in each review whether the summary answered her concern, and adjust the next one. Step 5: name an owner, the project manager.

Common mistake: sending the same long, detailed report to everyone on the same schedule, then reading silence as approval. Silence without a feedback route hides confusion.

Consequence: when the sponsor learns of a delay only at a quarterly review, funding decisions are made on stale facts and the recovery options have already shrunk.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT lead is running a billing system upgrade. The chief financial officer funds the work and has final say on its scope, and she needs to hear about any change that could push go-live past the quarter-end close. The team has completed these parts of the communication strategy: (1) her need is recorded as any change that could move go-live past quarter-end, flagged within three working days; (2) the format is a single-page table marking each workstream on track, at risk, or late; (3) the frequency is weekly on Monday, plus a same-day phone call for any late item; (5) the owner is the IT project lead. Which step is still missing, and what should it do?
choices: Add a feedback loop: in each review, ask the CFO whether the table answered her concern, and change the next table to match her reply.
Ask the CFO to approve the communication plan once and stop reviewing it, so updates can run on autopilot.
Send the full integration test log to all 200 hospital staff every week so nobody is surprised.
Move the frequency to daily emails to every workstream lead so that no delay goes unnoticed for a day.
questions.why: The missing step is the feedback loop, which is a deliberate route for the sponsor to reply so the team learns whether the update was understood and still useful.

questions.prompt: A water utility keeps live pump-station pressure readings on a shared screen. Engineers open it whenever they want to check a reading, and nobody is sent a copy. Which communication shape does this describe?
choices: Interactive, because the screen supports a two-way discussion
Interactive, because the engineers reply to the readings by logging their checks
Pull, because the information is left for people to fetch when they need it
Push, because the readings are sent to the engineers
questions.why: Information made available for people to fetch on their own schedule is pull, while push is sent to recipients and interactive is a two-way discussion.

questions.prompt: A charity's volunteer coordinator sends the same 12-page weekly report to donors and to volunteers. No one replies, so she assumes everyone understands it and is satisfied. What is the main flaw in her approach?
choices: The volunteers should be given a pull dashboard instead of any report at all.
She has no feedback route, so silence cannot tell her whether the message was understood or still useful.
The report should be sent in a different file format, such as a spreadsheet.
The report should be sent less often, because weekly reports always overwhelm people.
questions.why: Silence without a feedback route hides confusion, so the coordinator cannot know whether the one-size report is working for each audience.

questions.prompt: A bank's chief risk officer is the sponsor of a system change. She needs to hear about any compliance risk that could threaten the regulatory filing date, and the project team is designing its communication strategy from scratch. What should the team do first?
choices: Name the owner of every message, so that accountability is fixed before anything else is discussed.
Pick a channel, such as a shared intranet page, because the channel decides what the sponsor will read.
Record her need for compliance risks that could affect the filing date, and flag them early enough to act on.
Choose a fixed reporting frequency of once a month, which is the standard for most bank projects.
questions.why: A good strategy starts from each stakeholder's needs, so the team first records what the sponsor needs to know and by when, before choosing format, frequency, or owner.

lessons.explainPrompt: You are about to start a project with a new sponsor and several stakeholders who feel uninformed. Explain to a teammate how you would build the communication plan and its feedback loops, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the stakeholders and asking each one what decisions they make and what information they need to make them, rather than sending one weekly email to everyone. From that I would write a communication strategy covering, for each message, the audience, content, format, frequency and owner. Then I would add feedback loops, such as a short question in every review asking whether the report answered their concern, and a standing channel for urgent issues. The sponsor would get a brief report rated against milestones, while the working team gets detailed updates. The main tradeoff is effort: a tailored plan takes time to set up and must be maintained, and too many channels can fragment information. So I would review the plan at each milestone and retire any channel nobody uses.
rubricPoints: Defines the communication strategy by audience, content, format, frequency and owner
Starts from each stakeholder's decisions and information needs, not a single uniform schedule
Describes a feedback loop that confirms a message was understood and still useful
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as effort to maintain or fragmentation from too many channels

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises this objective, and explaining a tailored communication plan and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill.

lessons.plain: An integrated project management plan is the set of linked plans that says how a project will be run from start to finish, covering scope, time, cost, quality, people, risk, and communication, so that all of them agree with one another. Before writing it, a project manager asks two questions: how complicated is this work, and which way of working suits it? A predictive approach plans most of the work up front and then follows that plan. An adaptive approach works in short cycles and adjusts as the team learns. A hybrid approach mixes the two. The manager also needs a realistic idea of how much effort the work will take, so people can plan and make decisions. This lesson covers how to judge complexity, choose an approach, and estimate effort, and why each choice matters once the work begins.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a new mobile app for a customer who is still unsure which features they want, and the launch date is fixed to a trade show. Would you plan every detail up front, work in short adjustable cycles, or mix the two? Give one reason for your choice.
lessons.teach: The integrated project management plan is the combined set of plans that governs a project. It describes how the work will be delivered, how changes are handled, and how the other plans fit together, so a change in one area, such as scope, is checked against its effect on schedule, cost, and quality. Complexity is how hard the work is to predict. It rises with the number of interdependent parts, the amount of uncertainty in requirements, the number of stakeholders with different views, new technology, and fixed constraints such as a firm date. A predictive approach suits work with stable, well understood requirements where changes are expensive: you plan up front and measure actual progress against the plan. An adaptive approach suits work with uncertain or changing requirements: you deliver small increments in short iterations and inspect and adjust after each one. A hybrid approach uses predictive planning for the parts that need fixed sign-off, such as hardware or regulated approvals, and adaptive cycles for the rest. The reason this works is that the way you plan should match how predictable the work is. Rigid planning on uncertain work produces expensive rework, while loose planning on fixed-compliance work produces late surprises. Effort estimation should give a range, not one number. A three-point estimate uses an optimistic value (O), a most likely value (M), and a pessimistic value (P), and combines them as (O + 4M + P) / 6. For example, a task with O = 3 days, M = 5 days, and P = 13 days gives (3 + 20 + 13) / 6 = 6 days. A common mistake is treating a single guessed number as a firm commitment and forgetting the assumptions behind it. If effort is underestimated, the plan is unrealistic from the start, and every later status report shows an overrun that was built in before any work began.

questions.prompt: A small print shop estimates a binding task with optimistic O = 4 hours, most likely M = 7 hours, and pessimistic P = 16 hours. Worked so far: Step 1, multiply M by 4 to get 28. Step 2, add O + 4M + P: 4 + 28 + 16 = 48. Step 3 is missing. What completes the three-point estimate?
choices: Divide the total of 48 by 6 to get 8 hours, the weighted estimate
Keep the total of 48 hours as the estimate, since it already includes all three values
Divide the total of 48 by 4, because M was weighted by 4
Take the average of O and P, which is 10 hours, and treat that as the commitment
questions.why: The formula (O + 4M + P) / 6 ends with dividing the combined total by 6, which gives 48 / 6 = 8 hours.

questions.prompt: A city council is building a parking-permit app. Its payment and accessibility-audit screens must pass a fixed regulatory sign-off, while the layout of the resident-facing screens is still being shaped by user feedback. Which way of working best fits the integrated plan described in the teaching text?
choices: A hybrid approach: predictive planning for the audit-gated screens and adaptive cycles for the feedback-driven screens
A purely adaptive approach for the whole app, because any fixed sign-off can be handled at the end
A purely predictive approach for the whole app, because a regulated product must be fully specified before any build starts
A single long predictive plan with no iterations, since adaptive cycles cannot coexist with compliance work
questions.why: The teaching text says hybrid uses predictive planning for parts needing fixed sign-off and adaptive cycles for the rest, which matches this split.

questions.prompt: A team estimates a data-migration task at O = 2 days, M = 5 days, and P = 14 days. Using the three-point method, what is the estimate, and what should the team keep alongside that number?
choices: 8 days, and only the pessimistic value, because it is the safest commitment
6 days, and the assumptions behind the O, M and P values, so later overruns can be traced
5 days, and nothing else, because the most likely value is the best single figure
7 days, and the optimistic value, because a midpoint is always the most realistic
questions.why: The weighted result is (2 + 20 + 14) / 6 = 6 days, and the teaching text warns that a single number without its assumptions hides where a later overrun came from.

questions.prompt: A warehouse project with a fixed reopening date proposes changing the shelf-bin sizes after the install plan was approved. The project manager checks only whether the change adds scope. What is the most important gap in that check, according to the integrated plan idea?
choices: It should be checked only against cost, because schedule and quality always stay fixed once a plan is approved
It should be approved immediately, since any change to shelf sizes is cheaper than checking its effects
It should be checked against schedule, cost and quality, because a scope change affects those other plans too
Nothing is missing, because bin sizes are part of scope and scope is the only plan that matters for a change
questions.why: The teaching text says a change in one area such as scope must be checked against its effect on schedule, cost and quality, so checking scope alone is the gap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a predictive, adaptive, or hybrid approach for a new project, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by judging how predictable the work is. I look at how stable the requirements are, how many parts depend on each other, whether there are fixed dates or regulated sign-offs, and how many stakeholders need to agree. If requirements are clear and changes would be costly, I lean predictive. If they are still being discovered, I lean adaptive with short cycles and regular reviews. If part of the work is fixed, such as hardware or an approval gate, and part is uncertain, I choose hybrid and keep the two parts clearly separated. For effort, I give ranges rather than single numbers, using optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values, and I write down the assumptions behind them. The tradeoff with an adaptive choice is that the final scope and cost are less certain, so stakeholders must accept that and see progress regularly. The tradeoff with predictive is that changes later are harder to absorb.
rubricPoints: Names the factors that drive complexity, such as uncertainty, interdependence, stakeholders, and fixed constraints
Matches predictive, adaptive, or hybrid to how predictable the requirements and constraints are
Explains effort as a range with stated assumptions, not a single guessed number
States a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen approach

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying an approach and an estimate is a reasoning skill best shown by explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers project planning directly.

lessons.plain: Scope is the agreed list of work a project must finish to deliver its result, and the rule that keeps that list from quietly growing. Managing scope means three things: writing the list down, getting the people who care about the project to agree to it, and breaking the big list into smaller pieces that can be checked. Think of renovating a kitchen. Before anyone picks up a tool, you write down that the room gets new cabinets and a sink but not a new floor, the owner signs it, and you split the job into cabinets, plumbing, and painting so each part can be estimated and finished. When the owner later asks for a new floor, you can see clearly that it is a change to the agreement, not a small favor.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is asked to 'build a new reporting feature' and starts coding the same day. Before you learn any terms here, what do you think would go wrong, and what is the first thing you would write down?
lessons.teach:
Scope is the agreed set of work and deliverables a project must produce, and it includes what is explicitly left out. Managing scope has three jobs: define it in writing, gain stakeholder agreement to it, and decompose it into smaller parts. Stakeholders are anyone who affects or is affected by the project, such as the sponsor, the users, and the operations staff. The written definition is the project scope statement. It describes the deliverables, lists what is out of scope, and gives acceptance criteria, which are the conditions that show a deliverable is good enough. Decomposition means breaking deliverables into smaller parts. The result is a work breakdown structure, or WBS, a tree in which the whole project sits at the top and each level splits the level above. The lowest pieces are work packages, small enough to estimate, assign, and check. A WBS dictionary records a short description for each element. The approved statement, the WBS, and the dictionary together form the scope baseline, the fixed reference point against which later changes are judged.

Worked example: a team builds a fleet dashboard. Step 1: the statement lists 'a dashboard showing daily fuel use per depot' and excludes driver payroll. Step 2: the first split is data feed, charts, and access controls. Step 3: charts split into a fuel-use chart, a depot table, and an export. Step 4: the export becomes a work package with an acceptance criterion that its CSV totals match the source data. Step 5: the sponsor and the operations lead review and sign off, which establishes the baseline.

Common mistake: splitting the WBS by phase (design, build, test) or by team instead of by deliverable. Then pieces overlap and nothing is clearly finished. Validating scope, meaning formal acceptance of deliverables by stakeholders, is also different from checking quality; a deliverable can be technically correct and still not be what was agreed.

Consequence: without a baseline, every new request looks like scope creep and cannot be judged. With one, each change goes through change control, where its effect on time and cost is visible before work starts. A baseline makes scope a decision, not an accident.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team is building a picking app for three distribution sites. Step 1: the scope statement describes a handheld picking app and a daily late-pick report, and it excludes returns processing. Step 2: the first split is handheld app, sync service, and reporting. Step 3: reporting splits into a stock-count report, a late-pick list, and an export. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: the sponsor and the warehouse supervisor review the WBS and sign off, which establishes the baseline. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 4?
choices: The team divides the sync service by developer, so each engineer owns one part of the WBS.
The team adds a schedule and cost estimate for the returns module, which was excluded in Step 1.
The team rewrites the scope statement to add returns processing before the sign-off in Step 5.
The export is broken down into work packages small enough to estimate and assign, and each gets an acceptance criterion such as the exported row count matching the warehouse system.
questions.why: Step 4 continues decomposition down to work packages with acceptance criteria, so each piece is small enough to estimate, assign, and check before sign-off.

questions.prompt: Which scope document lists what is out of scope and gives the acceptance criteria for each deliverable?
choices: The project scope statement
The work breakdown structure
The WBS dictionary
The scope baseline
questions.why: The scope statement describes the deliverables, lists exclusions, and gives acceptance criteria; the dictionary only holds short descriptions and the baseline is the combined approved set.

questions.prompt: A school-construction team splits its WBS into design, build, and inspect phases. What is the most likely result?
choices: The WBS becomes a schedule and no longer needs a dictionary.
Every deliverable is clearly finished at the end of its phase.
The scope statement must be rewritten to remove out-of-scope items.
Pieces overlap and it becomes unclear when any deliverable is done.
questions.why: Splitting by phase instead of by deliverable makes pieces overlap, so nothing is clearly finished, which is the common mistake the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A clinic scheduling system passes every technical test, but the nurse manager says it does not match what was agreed. Which step is still needed?
choices: Formal acceptance by stakeholders against the agreed criteria, because technical correctness alone does not show the deliverable is what was agreed.
A new WBS split by team so that the nurses own their own pieces.
Change control, because this is scope creep and must be judged before any work is done.
The team has passed quality checks, so it should close the work package and move on without further review.
questions.why: Validation is formal stakeholder acceptance against agreed criteria, which is separate from quality checks, so a technically correct deliverable can still be rejected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a project needs an agreed scope baseline and how decomposing scope into work packages helps. Name one limit or tradeoff of breaking scope down too finely.
lessons.modelAnswer: A scope baseline is the approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary, and it gives the team a fixed reference point. Without it, every request looks like a reasonable addition, and nobody can tell whether time and cost are drifting. Decomposing scope into work packages turns a vague goal like 'build the dashboard' into pieces that can each be estimated, assigned, and checked against acceptance criteria, so progress is visible. The tradeoff is that over-decomposing creates many tiny packages, which adds tracking overhead and can hide the big picture. Each package also needs its own estimate and status update, so the team should stop splitting once a piece is small enough to estimate and verify with reasonable confidence.
rubricPoints: Scope baseline is the agreed reference point used to judge changes
Decomposition turns deliverables into estimable, checkable work packages
Acceptance criteria and stakeholder sign-off define when work is done
A stated limit or tradeoff, such as overhead from over-decomposition

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scope-change scenario in an exam-style situation adds the most for this objective, since none of the current missions cover project scope.

lessons.plain: Value-based delivery means making sure the project's work actually produces the results it was meant to produce, not just finishing tasks on a list. A project manager first names the value components, meaning the specific benefits the work is supposed to bring, such as faster order handling or fewer customer complaints. Then work is ordered so the pieces that deliver the most value, and that teach the team the most from early feedback, come first. Finally, the manager checks that someone is measuring those benefits over time, using a simple tracking method with an owner and a review schedule. Without that check, a project can deliver everything on time and still change nothing for the people it was for.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team delivered a new reporting feature on schedule and within budget, but three months later nobody uses it and the support queue is unchanged. Which step, if it had been in place, would most likely have revealed this earlier, and why?
lessons.teach:
A value component is a specific benefit the project is meant to produce, paired with a measure that shows whether it happened. A benefits-tracking system is the agreed way of collecting those measures: the metric, its baseline (the value before the project), its target, a named owner, and a fixed review schedule. Prioritizing by value and feedback means ranking work by expected benefit compared with cost and risk, and sequencing short pieces of work so that real users respond early and the ranking can be corrected.

Worked example. A dispatch software project has three candidate features. Feature A, a live map for dispatchers, is tied to the value component missed pickups, measured as missed pickups per thousand jobs; the baseline is 40 and the target is 15. Feature B, automatic invoice export, saves finance staff time, a smaller benefit with low cost. Feature C, driver photo upload, has no measured link to any benefit. Step one: write the value component and metric for each. Step two: rank A first because its expected benefit is highest for moderate cost. Step three: deliver A in a two-week slice and gather dispatcher feedback before building more. Step four: confirm the missed-pickup baseline was captured before release, the metric has an owner, and a monthly review is booked.

A common mistake is treating shipped features as benefits. Counting 'feature delivered' as success says nothing about whether dispatchers miss fewer pickups. In a running system, if no baseline was captured, the team cannot later show whether the change worked, so the project closes as successful on paper while the original problem persists.

Value is only real when it is measured, and measurement must be set up before the work ships.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank has three candidate tools. Tool 1, a pickup-reminder text for partner pantries, is tied to the value component missed deliveries, measured as missed deliveries per hundred scheduled drops. Its baseline is 18, its target is 6, an owner named Dev Rao holds it, and a monthly review is booked. Tool 2, an automated donor thank-you email, saves office staff about one hour a week at low cost. Tool 3, a redesigned printed sign-in sheet, has no measured link to any benefit. The team ranks Tool 1 first, delivers it to two pantries as a one-week slice, and collects their feedback. Step four, which the team must complete before building more, is missing. Which choice completes it?
choices: Re-rank the remaining work using the pantry feedback and the missed-delivery measure, then pick the next slice.
Build Tool 2 and Tool 3 in full so all benefits ship together.
Reset the missed-delivery baseline to the first week's figure.
Close the project because the first slice shipped on schedule.
questions.why: Sequencing short slices lets real users respond early so the ranking of remaining work can be corrected before more effort is spent.

questions.prompt: In a benefits-tracking system, what is the baseline for a metric?
choices: The measured value of the metric before the project changes anything.
The total cost of collecting the metric across the life of the project.
The target value the project must reach by its closing date.
The named person who is accountable for reviewing the metric each month.
questions.why: The baseline is the value captured before the project, which later lets the team compare results against it.

questions.prompt: A council permit office has three candidate changes: an online status page expected to cut phone calls by a measured 300 a month at low cost and low risk, a scanner upgrade with high cost and unknown benefit, and a new logo on forms with no measurable link to any benefit. Which should be sequenced first in a short slice?
choices: The logo change, since it is the quickest of the three to deliver to users.
All three together, so that no ranking is needed and nothing is left out.
The scanner upgrade, since its high cost means it must be proven before anything else is attempted.
The online status page, which has a measurable benefit at low cost and risk.
questions.why: Ranking by expected benefit relative to cost and risk puts the status page first, and a short slice lets users confirm the ranking early.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team delivers a picking-accuracy change and closes the project citing feature delivered as success. No baseline for picking errors was captured before release. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: The change will be credited with the benefit automatically once staff begin using it every day.
Staff will stop using the feature because it was released without any accompanying training material.
The team will have to repeat the whole project before it can request funding for the next phase.
Nobody can show whether picking errors fell, so the original problem may persist while the project reads as successful.
questions.why: Without a baseline the team cannot compare before and after, so counting shipped features hides whether the original problem was solved.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide what the project should build first, and how you would confirm that benefits are actually being tracked. Name one limit or tradeoff of ranking work by value.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the value components: for each planned piece of work, what benefit it should produce and how we would measure it, such as missed pickups per thousand jobs. Then I would rank the work by expected value compared with cost and risk, and put early the items that test our assumptions fastest, so we get feedback from dispatchers in the first couple of weeks rather than at the end. To confirm benefits tracking, I would check that a baseline was captured before release, that each measure has a named owner and a target, and that someone reviews it on a fixed schedule. The tradeoff is that value estimates are uncertain early on, and a high-value item may also be hard or risky, so I would revisit the ranking as feedback comes in rather than treating the first ranking as fixed.
rubricPoints: Names specific value components tied to measurable benefits, not just features.
Ranks work by expected value against cost and risk, and uses early feedback to reorder it.
Verifies a benefits-tracking system exists, with a baseline, target, owner and review schedule.
Names a limit, such as value estimates being uncertain early on or high-value work being risky.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises benefits tracking or value prioritization directly, so explaining the reasoning back is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: This objective covers the people, equipment and outside suppliers a project depends on, and the money that pays for them. You work out what each piece of work needs and when, decide whether to buy something from an outside company and on what kind of agreement, check how well that company performs, and keep spending tied to what was planned. Think of building a house: you book builders for the right weeks, choose whether to pay a fixed price for the kitchen or pay by the hour, and check that the bills match the progress made. Getting these choices right keeps a project from running out of people, money or a reliable supplier halfway through.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small team needs an outside specialist for a job whose requirements are still unclear. Would you rather agree to a fixed total price or pay for the actual hours worked, and why?
lessons.teach: Resource management means planning which people, equipment and materials the project needs, when they are needed, and whether they are actually available. A resource calendar records when each person or item can work. Resource leveling adjusts the schedule so nobody is overbooked, which usually lengthens the end date. Resource smoothing shifts work within the available slack so the end date stays the same. Procurement is the process of buying work or goods from an outside vendor, a seller who signs a contract with you. The contract type decides who carries the risk of cost overruns. In a fixed-price contract the seller agrees to a set total, so the seller absorbs extra cost, but this only works when the scope is well defined. In a cost-reimbursable contract the buyer pays the seller's actual costs plus a fee, so the buyer carries the cost risk, which suits uncertain work. Time and materials contracts pay agreed hourly or unit rates and sit between the two. Worked example: a team hires a vendor to build a reporting module. Step one, the requirements are clear and signed off. Step two, the team picks fixed price because the risk of overrun can sit with the vendor.
