Step three, during delivery the vendor is scored against agreed metrics such as defect count and on-time delivery, and that score informs the next award decision. Project finances are tracked with earned value. Planned value (PV) is the budget for work scheduled to date, earned value (EV) is the budget value of work actually completed, and actual cost (AC) is what was spent. The cost performance index (CPI) equals EV divided by AC; below 1 means you are getting less than one dollar of value for each dollar spent. Common mistake: choosing fixed price for vague scope. The vendor then either pads the price or raises change requests, and the resulting dispute slows the project. The contract type is a risk allocation decision, and it must match how well the work is understood.

questions.prompt: A distribution centre hires an installer to fit 120 metres of pallet racking, and the scope and drawings are signed off. The project manager tracks progress with earned value. At the week 8 review: planned value (PV) for the work scheduled to date is 40,000, earned value (EV) for racking actually installed is 32,000, and actual cost (AC) is 36,000. Step one: the team confirms the three figures are in the same currency and cover the same work. Step two: the team divides EV by AC to get the cost performance index (CPI), which is 32,000 divided by 36,000, about 0.89. Step three is missing: the team must state what the 0.89 means for the budget and what it calls for.
choices: Each dollar spent has bought about 89 cents of completed work, so costs are running over and the cause should be investigated.
The project is under budget because AC is lower than PV, so no action is needed this week.
The schedule is on track because EV is close to PV, so only the schedule index needs checking.
The installer should be paid a bonus because the CPI is below 1, which shows the work is cheaper than planned.
questions.why: A CPI below 1 means the value earned is less than the money spent, so the cost overrun must be investigated, and option 0 states exactly that interpretation.

questions.prompt: A plumbing firm has two senior technicians each booked on the same three days in a refurbishment project. The project manager must keep the finish date unchanged and only shift tasks that have spare time. Which technique fits, and why?
choices: Resource leveling, because it removes the overbooking and the end date stays the same.
Resource leveling, because it moves work outside the available slack so the end date is fixed.
Resource smoothing, because it adds a third technician and lengthens the end date.
Resource smoothing, because it moves work inside available slack so the end date stays the same.
questions.why: Smoothing shifts work within slack so the end date holds, while leveling removes overbooking but usually lengthens the end date.

questions.prompt: A council hires a contractor to resurface 2 km of road. The specification, quantities and standards are fully defined and agreed. The team chooses a cost-reimbursable contract. What is the main problem with that choice?
choices: The council carries the cost-overrun risk even though the work is well defined, when a fixed-price contract would move that risk to the contractor.
The council cannot score the contractor's performance under a cost-reimbursable contract, so the award cannot be informed.
There is no problem, because contract type has no effect on who carries cost risk when the specification is clear.
The contractor will pad the price, so a cost-reimbursable contract is the only way to protect the council from overruns.
questions.why: Cost-reimbursable contracts put cost risk on the buyer, which is unnecessary when scope is well defined and a fixed price could shift that risk to the seller.

questions.prompt: A school district has a network cabling vendor on a multi-phase contract. Each phase ends with a review of defect count and on-time delivery against agreed metrics. What should the district do with the review result?
choices: Pay a fixed bonus to the vendor in every phase regardless of the score, to keep the relationship stable.
Hold the scores until project close and only then review them, so the vendor is never influenced mid-contract.
Record the score against the agreed metrics and let it inform the next award decision.
Terminate the contract at the first late delivery without checking the metrics or the cause.
questions.why: Vendor performance is scored against agreed metrics during delivery and that score feeds the next award decision, so recording it against those metrics is the intended use.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a fixed-price and a cost-reimbursable contract for a new vendor, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking how well the work is defined. If the scope is clear and signed off, a fixed-price contract moves the cost-overrun risk to the vendor, so we know our total in advance. If the scope is uncertain, a fixed price invites padding or a stream of change requests, so I would prefer a cost-reimbursable contract, where we pay actual costs plus a fee and keep the risk ourselves. The tradeoff with cost-reimbursable is that our spending is less predictable, so we need tight monitoring, such as checking CPI against earned value each period, and clear limits on the fee. Whichever I pick, I would also set agreed performance metrics so we can score the vendor later.
rubricPoints: Fixed price suits well-defined scope and shifts cost risk to the seller
Cost-reimbursable suits uncertain scope and leaves cost risk with the buyer
The choice is a risk allocation that must match how well the work is understood
A named tradeoff or limit, such as unpredictable spend or padding, with a control to manage it

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers contract selection or earned value, so reasoning through an exam-style delivery scenario adds the most.

lessons.plain: Quality planning means deciding, before and during the work, what good enough means for the thing being delivered and how you will check for it. A project manager first gathers what the people who use or pay for the result actually need, turns those needs into measurable targets, writes down how checks will happen and who does them, then keeps running those checks and uses what they reveal to get better over time. Think of a restaurant: the owner decides what a good meal means, sets hygiene and temperature rules, inspects during service, and changes the kitchen when guests keep complaining about the same dish. The goal is to build quality in rather than inspect it in at the end.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team releases software and customers find three serious bugs a week after go-live. Before any teaching, what could the team have done earlier in the project to make those bugs less likely, and how would they know whether it was working?
lessons.teach:
Quality requirements are the specific conditions a deliverable must meet to be accepted, such as a page loading in under two seconds or a defect rate below a stated limit. They come from stakeholders, contracts, regulations and the organisation's own standards. They should be measurable, because a requirement nobody can check is only a wish.

A quality metric is the measurement used to check one requirement, for example the percentage of page loads that finish under two seconds. The quality management plan is the document describing how the team will plan, check and improve quality: which metrics it uses, how often it measures them, who inspects the work, and what happens when a measurement falls short.

Executing the plan means running those checks while the work is under way. Quality assurance checks that the way the team works is producing good results, such as confirming that code reviews really happen. Quality control compares the actual output against the metrics. Continuous improvement is the habit of using these results to change the process, often through a plan, do, check, act loop in which a small change is tried, measured, and kept only if it helps. Root cause analysis asks why a defect happened, not just how to patch it.

Worked example: the requirement is that at least 99.5 percent of sessions finish without a crash. In week one the team measures 98.7 percent. A root cause review finds most crashes come from one unhandled network timeout. The team adds a test for that timeout and a review checklist item, then measures again the next week and gets 99.6 percent. The change is kept and recorded.

Common mistake: treating quality as a final testing phase. Defects found just before release are the most expensive to fix, and a team that tests only at the end learns nothing about why the defects appeared. In a running system, a missing quality check shows up as incidents after deployment, when the cost is highest.

Quality planning builds checks in from the start and turns every measured shortfall into a process change.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team has a requirement that at least 98 percent of pallet labels scan correctly on the first attempt. A quality metric is the measurement used to check that requirement, here the share of labels that scan first time. In week one the team measures 96.2 percent. Next, a root cause analysis, which asks why a defect happened rather than only how to patch it, finds that most failed scans come from smudged labels printed by one older printer whose ribbon runs low. The team then adds a ribbon-check item to the start-of-shift routine and measures again the following week, getting 98.4 percent. The change is kept and recorded. The step missing from this account is the one between measuring the shortfall and making the change: the team had to ask why the labels smudged, which is the root cause review. Which step should fill that gap?
choices: Run a root cause review to find out why the labels smudged before choosing a fix
Add a final inspection of every pallet at the dock before shipping
Ask the night shift to work faster so fewer labels are printed in a rush
Raise the requirement to 99 percent so the team has a margin before the change is made
questions.why: The team must find why the defect happened before changing the process, and the root cause review is the step that does this.

questions.prompt: In quality management, which statement best describes quality assurance as opposed to quality control?
choices: Quality assurance and quality control are two names for the same final inspection.
Quality assurance checks that the way the team works is producing good results, while quality control compares actual output against the metrics.
Quality assurance measures the finished output against the metrics, while quality control checks how the team works.
Quality assurance sets the requirements, while quality control writes the quality management plan.
questions.why: Quality assurance examines the working process and quality control compares output to metrics, so the first option reverses the two definitions.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a requirement that at least 95 percent of parcels arrive within 24 hours. This week the metric reads 91 percent. The operations manager responds by adding an extra inspection of all parcels at the end of each week and says the team is now covered. What is the main failure in this response?
choices: The response is correct because inspection always raises the number of on-time parcels.
The inspection should happen on the first day of the week instead of the last.
The team should have lowered the requirement to match the 91 percent result.
The team has not checked whether the extra inspection changes the metric, and has not asked why parcels were late.
questions.why: Continuous improvement needs a root cause review and a measured change, and an end-of-week inspection finds problems after they have happened without addressing why the delays occur.

questions.prompt: A client contract says the new booking app must feel fast to users. Which rewrite of this requirement best meets the idea that a requirement should be measurable?
choices: The app should be quick and responsive for most people most of the time.
At least 95 percent of booking confirmations appear within 2 seconds, measured on a mid-range test phone over a standard mobile connection.
The app should be pleasant to use on a range of devices.
The app should be as fast as the competitor's app or better.
questions.why: Only the last option states a threshold, a share of cases, and a way to measure it, so anyone could check whether it was met.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how quality planning differs from testing at the end of a project, and name one limit or tradeoff of adding frequent quality checks.
lessons.modelAnswer: Quality planning starts before anything is built. We agree what acceptable means in measurable terms, write down how we will measure it and who checks, and then run those checks as the work goes on. Testing at the end is only one of those checks, and by then fixing a defect is expensive. The tradeoff is that frequent checks cost time and attention: every audit, review gate or measurement takes effort away from building. So I would tie the checks to the requirements that matter most, such as those affecting customer safety or contract acceptance, and reduce checks that have never caught anything. The quality management plan should state how often each check runs, so the team can see the cost and decide whether it earns its place. Improvement should come from what the results show, not from more inspection for its own sake.
rubricPoints: Quality planning sets measurable requirements before the work starts, rather than only testing at the end.
Checks run during execution through quality assurance and quality control, and their results feed improvement.
Frequent checks cost time, so they should be chosen against the requirements that matter most.
Each measured shortfall should lead to a root cause analysis and a documented process change.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the plan, check, and improve loop and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises quality management directly.

lessons.plain: Planning a schedule means working out how long each piece of work will take, putting those pieces in order, and saving a fixed copy of that plan as a yardstick called the baseline. Later you compare what actually happened against that copy. How you estimate depends on how the work is delivered. A plan that is fixed up front can use detailed time estimates drawn from similar past jobs, while a team working in short cycles estimates relative size and learns its pace from work it has finished. The gap between what was planned to be done by now and what is actually done is the schedule variance, and it tells you whether the project is ahead or behind.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's plan says half the work should be finished by Wednesday, and on Wednesday they have finished only a third of it. Without using any formulas, how would you describe how far behind they are, and what would you need to know before deciding this is a real problem rather than normal noise?
lessons.teach:
Baseline: the approved version of the schedule, frozen so later progress can be measured against it. Changing it should go through a formal change decision, not be done quietly. Planned value (PV): the budgeted value of the work the baseline says should be complete by a given date. Earned value (EV): the budgeted value of the work that is actually complete, measured by what was delivered, not by hours spent. Schedule variance (SV) equals EV minus PV. A negative number means behind. Schedule performance index (SPI) equals EV divided by PV; below 1 means slower than planned.

Estimating method should fit the delivery approach. In a predictive plan, analogous estimating borrows durations from similar past work, parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate by a quantity, and three-point estimating uses an optimistic, most likely and pessimistic figure, combined as (optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic) divided by six. In an adaptive team, work is sized in relative points and velocity, the average points finished per iteration, forecasts the remaining work.

Worked example: a 20-day plan. At day 10, PV is 10 days of budgeted work. The team has finished work worth 8 days, so EV is 8. SV is 8 minus 10, which is minus 2. SPI is 8 divided by 10, which is 0.8, so the work is running at 80 percent of plan.

Common mistake: comparing actual spend with plan and calling that schedule performance, or rebaselining every time a variance appears, which hides slippage. In a running delivery, unnoticed negative variance surfaces late, when recovery options are few.

questions.prompt: A delivery team finished 12, 15, 18 and 15 points in its last four iterations and has 75 points of work left. Step 1 is already done: velocity, the average points finished per iteration, is 15 points per iteration. Step 2 is the one left for you: using that velocity, how many more iterations does the forecast predict?
choices: 4 iterations
6 iterations
5 iterations
75 iterations
questions.why: The forecast divides the remaining points by the velocity, so 75 divided by 15 gives 5 iterations.

questions.prompt: A predictive team estimates a single task with three figures: optimistic 6 days, most likely 9 days, pessimistic 18 days. Using the three-point method, where the expected duration is (optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic) divided by six, what is the estimate?
choices: 10 days
8 days
9 days
12 days
questions.why: The sum is 6 plus 36 plus 18, which is 60, and 60 divided by 6 gives 10 days.

questions.prompt: A data migration is in week 6. The baseline says work worth 30,000 should be complete by now (planned value). The work actually delivered is worth 24,000 (earned value, measured by what was delivered), and 36,000 has been spent. Which statement about schedule variance is correct?
choices: Schedule variance is plus 6,000, because the team spent more than planned.
Schedule variance is minus 12,000, the gap between spend and earned value.
Schedule variance is minus 0.8, because that is the schedule performance index.
Schedule variance is minus 6,000, because earned value minus planned value is 24,000 minus 30,000.
questions.why: Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value, which is 24,000 minus 30,000, giving minus 6,000; the spend figure does not enter into it.

questions.prompt: A new mobile product team of six has no history of similar work and runs two-week iterations. Which estimating approach fits this adaptive setting?
choices: Multiply a cost rate per screen by the number of screens in the backlog.
Size backlog items in relative story points, then use the team's average points per iteration to forecast remaining work.
Build a three-point estimate from one engineer's optimistic, likely and pessimistic guesses.
Copy the durations of a similar predictive project completed by another department.
questions.why: Adaptive teams size work in relative points and forecast from velocity, which suits a team without historical data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate new to planning how we should estimate and track the schedule on a predictive project compared with an agile one, and name one limit of the schedule variance measure that you would keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: On a predictive project we freeze an approved baseline and estimate durations with methods such as analogous, parametric or three-point estimating, then measure progress with planned value, earned value, schedule variance and the schedule performance index. On an agile project we size work in relative points, measure velocity over iterations, and forecast the remaining backlog from that pace instead of a detailed fixed calendar. One limit of schedule variance is that it measures value completed against the plan's sequence, not whether the remaining work is still valid. A project can show a small variance while the scope has quietly grown, or it can look behind because early estimates were optimistic. So I would read variance alongside the forecast and the scope changes, not as a verdict on its own.
rubricPoints: Predictive work uses a fixed baseline and estimating methods such as analogous, parametric or three-point estimating
Adaptive work sizes items relatively and forecasts from velocity over iterations
Schedule variance equals earned value minus planned value, and the performance index is earned value divided by planned value
Variance has limits: it does not show whether scope or estimates are still valid

suggested.rationale: Choosing an estimating method and reading variance numbers in a delivery scenario is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations, and no listed mission covers schedule control directly.

lessons.plain: Evaluating project status means checking, with evidence, whether a project is on track, and then telling the right people in a form they can use. A project metric is a number that measures something you care about, such as how much work is finished, how many problems are open, or how far spending has moved from plan. An artifact is any document or record the project produces, like a decision log or a risk register. Keeping artifacts accessible means the team and stakeholders can find the current version without asking around. Communicating status means sharing those facts on a schedule, in a format that fits each audience.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project manager reports 'green' every week, but the launch date keeps slipping. What would you check first to judge whether 'green' is honest, and why?
lessons.teach:
A project metric is a measured number that tells you something about progress, quality, cost, or risk. A baseline is the agreed plan you measure against, such as the number of items planned to be finished by a given week. A status report is a regular summary that compares current measures to the baseline, explains any gap, and states what will be done about it. An artifact is any record the project produces, such as a status log, a risk register, or a decision log. Accessible means the current version lives in one agreed place that the team and stakeholders can open without asking someone for it.

Why it works: a number compared with a baseline shows direction. 'We feel fine' cannot be checked; 'seven of ten planned items are done and open defects rose from four to eleven' can be questioned and acted on.

Worked example: a team building a billing feature planned 10 finished items by week 3. Step 1: count the finished items, which is 7. Step 2: compute the gap, 3 items or 30 percent behind. Step 3: check a second metric, open defects, which rose from 4 to 11. Step 4: report amber, with the cause, a recovery plan, and a decision needed from the sponsor. Step 5: save the report with its date in the shared log.

Common mistake: reporting activity such as hours logged or meetings held as if it were progress, or reporting one overall color with no measure behind it.

Consequence: if the sponsor hears only 'green' until go-live, a slip that was visible in week 3 arrives as a surprise when there is little room left to recover.

questions.prompt: A school district is rolling out 600 laptops across six campuses. The agreed baseline is 40 laptops imaged and handed out by day 30. Step 1: count the finished handouts, which is 31. Step 2: compute the gap, 9 laptops or 22.5 percent behind. Step 3: check a second metric, help-desk tickets about setup, which rose from 12 to 35 that week. Step 4: report amber, with the cause, a recovery plan, and a decision needed from the superintendent. What is step 5?
choices: Keep the report in the coordinator's personal folder and send it only when the rollout finishes
Overwrite last week's report so the file always holds only the newest numbers
Log the 90 technician hours spent this week as evidence that the rollout is moving
Save the dated report in the one shared log that staff and the superintendent can open without asking for it
questions.why: Step 5 is the accessibility step: the current dated version must sit in one agreed place that the team and stakeholders can open on their own.

questions.prompt: Which of these best defines a project metric?
choices: A summary sent to the sponsor at the end of each month
Any folder where the team keeps its project files
A measured number about progress, quality, cost, or risk
The agreed plan you measure against, such as items due by a set week
questions.why: A project metric is a measured number that tells you something about progress, quality, cost, or risk; the other options describe a baseline, a status report, and a storage location.

questions.prompt: A team reports 'Green: 280 hours logged this sprint and six meetings held.' What is the main problem with this report?
choices: The report only needs a defect count added, and nothing else is wrong
Hours and meetings are activity, not measured progress, and nothing is compared with a baseline
Meetings should be counted only in cost metrics
Green is the wrong color because logged hours always signal risk
questions.why: Reporting activity as if it were progress, with no comparison to an agreed baseline, is the common mistake the text warns about, so the report cannot be checked.

questions.prompt: A team says the project 'feels on track', and its risk register sits in two different folders with different versions. Which pair of changes addresses both problems?
choices: Ask the team to rate their confidence each week and keep both folders
Give the sponsor a single green rating and archive the older folder
Replace the feeling with a number compared to a baseline, and keep one current version in one agreed shared place
Add daily meetings so status is discussed more often, and keep both folders
questions.why: A number compared with a baseline shows direction, and an accessible artifact is the current version in one agreed place that people can open without asking for it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we don't need a status report because everyone can see the board. Explain to them what a status report adds, and name one limit of relying only on metrics.
lessons.modelAnswer: A board shows which tasks are in which column, but it doesn't say whether we are on track against the plan we agreed, or why. A status report takes a few measures, such as planned versus finished items and open defects, compares them to the baseline, and explains the gap and the action we are taking. It also states which decision stakeholders need to make, which a board never does. The limit is that numbers can mislead on their own. A count of finished items says nothing about whether the finished work is the valuable part, so I would pair each metric with a short explanation and check it with the people doing the work before I send it.
rubricPoints: Says a status report compares measures against an agreed baseline, not just shows the current state.
Names what the report adds: an explanation of the gap, a recovery action, and any decisions needed.
Names a real limit of metrics, such as numbers lacking context or saying nothing about quality or value.
Mentions keeping the report in an accessible, dated, shared location.

suggested.rationale: A status-reporting scenario where a dashboard conflicts with the plan is best reasoned through, since no listed mission practices status communication.

lessons.plain: Closing a project means finishing it on purpose rather than just stopping work. Before you let go, the people who asked for the work must formally agree it is done, the thing you built must be ready for whoever will run it, and the leftover business must be tidied up. That means settling supplier contracts, reconciling money, releasing people and equipment, and writing down what the team learned for next time. Closure is the last chance to check the result against what was promised, so skipping it leaves loose ends that surface months later.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has finished building a new reporting tool, and everyone is relieved and ready to move on to the next project. Before the project is marked finished, what do you think still has to happen, and who would you need to hear from?
lessons.teach:
Project closure is the set of activities that formally ends a project or phase. A stakeholder is any person or group with an interest in the project or influence over it, such as a sponsor, a customer, or the operations team that will run the result. Obtaining stakeholder approval means getting a documented sign-off that the deliverables meet the agreed requirements. Transition readiness means checking that the product can be handed over: support documents exist, people have been trained, and the receiving team has accepted ownership. Closeout activities tidy the remaining business. Procurement closeout settles and archives supplier contracts. Financial closeout reconciles actual spending against the budget and closes the cost records. Resource closeout releases team members and equipment back to their home groups. Lessons learned is a written record of what worked and what did not, and a retrospective is a short group review that produces that record.

Why it works: a project is only finished when someone with authority has accepted the result and someone else can keep it running. Without both, work quietly returns to the original team as unplanned support.

Worked example: a team builds a vehicle-tracking dashboard. First, the sponsor checks the acceptance criteria against the original requirements and signs the acceptance record. Second, operations confirms the runbook and alert setup are in place and formally takes ownership. Third, finance reconciles the final vendor invoice and closes the purchase order. Fourth, the team holds a retrospective and files the lessons learned in the project archive. Only after all four steps is the project closed.

Common mistake: treating the production deployment as closure. A product that is live but has no signed acceptance and no owner is still an open project, and the team will keep answering requests indefinitely.

Consequence: if the vendor contract stays open, billing can continue unnoticed, and if no one owns the service, the first outage lands on the old team with no agreed way to respond. Closure is what turns a delivered system into an operated one.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank builds a volunteer scheduling app with an outside software firm. Five closure steps are finished. First, the executive director compares the app against the 14 agreed requirements and signs the acceptance record. Second, the volunteer coordinator confirms the user guide is written and formally takes ownership of the app. Third, the team settles the firm's licence contract and archives it. Fourth, the 6 contract developers are released back to the firm and the 2 borrowed tablets are returned to the warehouse. Fifth, the team holds a short retrospective and files the lessons learned. One closure step is still missing: the finance lead has not compared the final amount actually spent with the approved budget or closed the cost records. The project cannot be called closed until that step is done.
choices: Publish the app on the public website so volunteers can start using it
Reconcile the actual spending against the approved budget and close the cost records
Hold a second sign-off from the software firm's sales team
Hold a retrospective to gather the lessons learned
questions.why: Financial closeout means reconciling actual spending against the budget and closing the cost records, and it is the one step in the scenario that has not been done.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's route planner has been handed over to its dispatch team. Which description best matches transition readiness?
choices: Support documents exist, people have been trained, and the receiving team has accepted ownership
The contractors have been released back to their home department
The sponsor has signed a record that the deliverables match the agreed requirements
The total budget has been compared with the amount actually spent
questions.why: Transition readiness is the check that the product can be handed over, which means support documents exist, staff are trained, and the receiving team has accepted ownership.

questions.prompt: A payroll tool at a manufacturing firm went live in production last week. Users are logging in and the team is answering questions daily. There is no signed acceptance record and the operations group has not agreed to own the tool. What is the correct status of the project?
choices: Closed, because the tool is running in production
Still open, because deployment alone does not provide acceptance or an owner
Closed, because the team has answered every user question
Closed for the business but open for the project team
questions.why: A product that is live without signed acceptance and a named owner is still an open project, because the team will keep receiving requests as unplanned support.

questions.prompt: A small architecture practice finished a client's building-permit tracker. The practice used a cloud hosting provider under a monthly contract and has now stopped using that provider. Which closeout activity applies to this contract?
choices: Transition readiness, which checks that support documents exist
Procurement closeout, which settles and archives the supplier contract
Resource closeout, which releases the team members to other groups
Lessons learned, which records what worked and what did not
questions.why: Procurement closeout is the activity that settles and archives supplier contracts, so the hosting provider's contract falls under it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that once the software is deployed to production, the project is done and people can be reassigned today. Explain to them what closure requires beyond deployment, and name one tradeoff of closing the project quickly versus closing it carefully.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deployment only shows the product is running. Closure also needs formal stakeholder acceptance, meaning the sponsor signs off that the deliverables match the agreed requirements. It needs transition readiness, meaning operations has the runbook, training and alerts, and has accepted ownership of the service. It also needs closeout of the business side: supplier contracts settled, the budget reconciled, resources released, and a retrospective whose lessons are written down. The tradeoff is that closing quickly frees people sooner and lowers overhead, but it risks open invoices, unowned support, and lessons that are never captured. Closing carefully costs some time and keeps everyone accountable for the result after the team moves on.
rubricPoints: Deployment alone is not closure; formal stakeholder acceptance is required.
Transition readiness means the receiving team can operate and own the product.
Procurement, financial and resource closeout must be completed.
Lessons learned or a retrospective should be recorded, and a tradeoff of speed versus thoroughness is named.

suggested.rationale: Closure is mostly a set of judgment calls about readiness and sign-off, and explaining the required steps and tradeoffs back to a teammate tests that understanding better than a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Project governance is the set of rules, roles, reporting habits and decision paths that decide how a project is directed and controlled. Think of it as the house rules of a project: who decides what, how often the sponsor hears the truth, what counts as a problem big enough to go up a level, and how the team behaves when no one is watching. Good governance does not make a project faster by itself, but it stops small problems from quietly becoming big ones, and it gives people a clear answer when they ask who can approve this.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team lead notices a supplier is running two weeks behind on a key delivery. Without being told any rules, what do you think should happen next, and who should hear about it first?
lessons.teach:
Governance is the framework that sets who decides what on a project and how decisions, information and problems move between people. Its parts are the structure (the roles, such as sponsor, steering committee and project manager), the rules (what needs approval and who gives it), the reporting (what is shared, how often, and in what format) and the ethics (the professional conduct expected of the team, including honest status). An escalation path is the route a problem takes upward. An escalation threshold is the measurable trigger that tells you when to take that route, which turns a judgement call into a test you can apply in minutes.

Why it works: decisions made at the lowest level that has the authority, with a known trigger for going higher, keep speed and control together. Without a threshold, people either escalate everything and overload the sponsor, or escalate nothing and bad news arrives late.

Worked example. A supplier's hardware delivery, planned for day 60 of a 60-day activity, is now 15 days late, and a milestone depends on it. Step 1: measure the variance. 15 out of 60 is 25 percent. Step 2: compare to the policy threshold, which says any schedule variance above 10 percent, or any milestone impact, goes to the steering committee within two business days. Both conditions are met. Step 3: the project manager raises it through the steering committee path, not directly to a senior executive who has been bypassing the committee. Step 4: the item is logged in the issue log with an owner and a decision date.

Common mistake: writing thresholds that are vague, such as 'significant delay', so each person applies a different meaning. Another is the project manager quietly absorbing the breach to protect the team's reputation.

Consequence: when a breach is hidden, the sponsor learns of the delay after the budget or the date has already been committed to the customer, and the options that would have worked earlier are gone.

questions.prompt: A warehouse software team runs a predictive project with a policy that says any draw on the contingency reserve above 10 percent, or any impact on a regulatory filing date, goes to the steering committee within three business days. A vendor raises its license fee by 12,000 currency units. The remaining contingency reserve is 90,000 units. Step 1: the team measures the draw, 12,000 out of 90,000, which is 13.3 percent. Step 2: the team compares this with the 10 percent threshold, and the threshold is exceeded. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the change is recorded in the issue log with an owner and a decision date. Which completes Step 3?
choices: The project manager approves the fee because the total project budget has not changed.
The team waits for the next monthly status report before telling anyone about the fee.
The project manager sends the item to the steering committee within three business days.
The project manager asks the vendor to absorb the fee so the reserve is not touched.
questions.why: The threshold has been breached, so the policy's escalation path requires routing the item to the steering committee within the stated three business days.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an escalation path and an escalation threshold?
choices: A path and a threshold are two names for the same governance document.
A path is the list of project roles, and a threshold is the schedule of status meetings.
A path is the route a problem takes upward, and a threshold is the measurable trigger that tells you to use it.
A path is a measurable trigger, and a threshold is the route a problem takes upward.
questions.why: The escalation path is the route upward, while the threshold is the measurable trigger that tells you when to take that route.

questions.prompt: A project charter says problems that cause a significant overrun must be escalated. Two team leads disagree about whether a 7 percent overrun counts. What is the core weakness of this rule?
choices: It fails to define a measurable trigger, so each person applies a different meaning and escalation becomes inconsistent.
It gives the project manager too much authority over the budget.
It does not name a sponsor who can approve the escalation.
It is written in a way that does not require a status report each week.
questions.why: A vague term like significant overrun lacks a measurable trigger, so people reach different conclusions about when to escalate.

questions.prompt: On a hybrid project, the policy says any milestone end date that moves more than 5 business days, or any change touching a safety control, goes to the steering committee. A sprint team finds that a safety interlock change will not move any milestone but must be built in the next sprint. What should the team do under the policy?
choices: Route the change to the steering committee, because it touches a safety control and the second condition applies regardless of dates.
Keep the change inside the sprint, since no milestone moves and the policy only applies to dates.
Log the change in the sprint retrospective and review it at the next retrospective.
Ask the product owner to decide alone, since the product owner owns the sprint backlog.
questions.why: The policy has two independent triggers, and a change touching a safety control meets the second one even though no milestone date moves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how project governance decides when a problem goes to the sponsor, and name one limit or tradeoff of setting escalation thresholds too tightly or too loosely.
lessons.modelAnswer: Governance is the set of rules that tells us who decides what and how problems travel upward. The practical piece is the escalation threshold: a measurable trigger, such as a schedule variance above 10 percent or any impact on a milestone, that moves an issue to the steering committee within a set time. You do not ask whether something feels serious; you check the number. The tradeoff is in how tight you set it. Set thresholds too tight and the committee is flooded with minor items, so real risks get buried and people stop trusting the process. Set them too loose and the sponsor hears about problems after the options have gone. A good threshold is one the team can measure without debate, and it should be reviewed after a few months against what actually surprised us.
rubricPoints: Governance defines structure, decision rights, reporting and ethics for the project
An escalation path is the route a problem takes upward, and a threshold is the measurable trigger for using it
Thresholds should be measurable so people apply them the same way
Tradeoff: too tight floods the committee and buries real risks; too loose delays bad news to the sponsor

suggested.rationale: Explaining the threshold-and-path logic back to a teammate, including its tradeoff, is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Compliance means a project follows the rules that apply to it: laws, safety standards, security requirements, environmental limits, and the organisation's own policies. Planning for compliance means finding out which of those rules touch your project, sorting them into groups so the right people own them, and working out what happens if the project breaks one. A project manager does not need to be the lawyer or the safety engineer, but must make sure the rules are known, written down, checked, and escalated when they are at risk. Think of it like building a house: the inspector's rules exist before the first wall goes up, not after.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team is about to store customers' personal data in a new cloud region. Before any design work starts, what compliance questions would you raise, and who would you ask to answer them?
lessons.teach:
A compliance requirement is a condition the project must meet because a law, regulation, standard, contract, or internal policy says so. Requirements used here fall into four groups. Security requirements protect data and systems from unauthorised access. Health and safety requirements protect people who build, operate, or use the output. Sustainability requirements set environmental limits such as emissions, waste, or energy use. Regulatory requirements come from a government or sector authority, such as privacy or financial reporting law. Classifying means sorting each requirement into one of these groups so it gets the right owner and the right checks.

Why it works: a requirement that is not written down cannot be tested, and a requirement with no owner tends to be missed. Confirming requirements before design is locked in is far cheaper than retrofitting them later.

Worked example: a project will move customer payment records to a new hosting region. Step 1: list the rules that touch it, such as a data protection law restricting where personal data may be stored (regulatory) and an access standard requiring encryption at rest (security). Step 2: classify each one. Step 3: assign an owner, such as the legal team for the storage rule and the security lead for encryption. Step 4: record the consequence of a breach, such as fines, suspension of the service, or loss of a contract. Step 5: schedule a compliance check before go-live.

Common mistake: treating compliance as a final review item. A check only at the end reveals a breach when it is most expensive to fix.

Consequence in a running system: a data-location breach may force an emergency migration or shutdown of the feature, and the breach may have to be reported within a legal time limit, so the escalation path matters as much as the rule itself.

Compliance is a property the project must be able to prove, not a feeling that it is probably fine.

questions.prompt: A regional council is rolling out 40 electric delivery vans with a telematics app that streams each driver's live location. Three rules apply. A workplace safety rule caps daily driving hours and must be enforced in the app (health and safety). A privacy law limits how long location history may be kept (regulatory). A council policy requires a 20 percent cut in fleet emissions by year end (sustainability). The team has listed all three rules and classified each one. The team has not yet assigned an owner to the location-retention rule, and that is the only step still missing for this rule. What should they do next?
choices: Reclassify the retention rule as sustainability, because keeping less data saves storage energy.
Assign the fleet manager as owner, since they see the location data every day.
Leave it without an owner until after launch, then check it during the first audit.
Assign the council's data protection officer as owner, since the rule comes from privacy law.
questions.why: A requirement that comes from a legal authority needs an owner who can answer for it to that authority, so the data protection officer is the right assignment, while the other choices either misclassify the rule or delay the check.

questions.prompt: A bakery is building an online ordering system. One requirement is that unauthorised staff must be blocked from viewing customers' stored card numbers. Which requirement group does this belong to?
choices: Sustainability, because it limits waste of stored data.
Health and safety, because staff could be harmed by data misuse.
Regulatory, because the bakery must follow a government rule.
Security, because it protects data from unauthorised access.
questions.why: Security requirements protect data and systems from unauthorised access, which is exactly what blocking staff from viewing card numbers does.

questions.prompt: A team is 80 percent through building a new employee-monitoring feature and only now starts listing the compliance rules that apply to it. Which response best follows sound compliance practice?
choices: Record the rules as policy notes only, because they cannot be tested anyway.
Ask the owner of each rule to test the finished feature during the next release.
Stop and confirm the requirements now, before the design is locked, because retrofitting them later is far more costly.
Finish the build first, since changes after go-live are normally cheaper to handle.
questions.why: The teaching states that confirming requirements before design is locked in is much cheaper than retrofitting them later, so confirming them now is the right move.

questions.prompt: A hospital's imaging team finds, after go-live, that patient scans are being stored in a location the regulator does not permit. Which consequence should the project plan for first?
choices: No consequence, because the storage rule was only a recorded policy.
A slower service that users will accept while the team fixes the design later.
A minor cosmetic report that can be filed at the next quarterly review.
A possible emergency migration or shutdown of the feature, plus a legal reporting deadline that the escalation path must meet.
questions.why: The teaching notes that a data-location breach may force an emergency migration or shutdown and may require reporting within a legal time limit, so the escalation path must be ready.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks compliance is the legal department's job how a project manager should plan for compliance requirements. Name one limit or tradeoff on how far the project manager should go.
lessons.modelAnswer: Compliance is shared, but the project manager owns making sure it is planned. Start by listing every rule that applies: laws, safety and security standards, environmental limits, and contract or policy obligations. Sort each one into a category such as security, health and safety, sustainability, or regulatory, so it lands with an owner who knows that area. Then, for each one, note what happens if it is broken: a fine, a shutdown, a contract penalty, or harm to people. That consequence tells you how much checking is needed and how fast to escalate. The limit is that the project manager does not interpret the law alone. Legal or safety specialists confirm what a rule means, and the project manager's job is to make sure those answers are recorded, scheduled into the plan, and not dropped in the rush to deliver.
rubricPoints: Identifies the applicable rules across security, health and safety, sustainability, and regulatory sources.
Classifies each requirement and assigns an owner with the expertise to confirm it.
Analyzes the consequence of noncompliance so checks and escalation are proportionate.
Names a limit: the project manager tracks and escalates while specialists interpret the rules.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style compliance scenario, sorting requirements and their consequences, adds more than any listed mission, since none covers compliance.

lessons.plain: When a project is underway, people will ask for changes: a new feature, a different supplier, a later deadline. Change control is the agreed routine for deciding which of these requests go ahead. Each request is written down, its effects on time, cost, quality and risk are estimated, and a named group makes a decision: approve, reject, or defer. Only approved changes may alter the agreed plan, and everyone who depends on that plan hears the outcome and the records get updated. It is less about saying no and more about making sure every yes is visible and deliberate.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor casually asks the team to add one extra report to the delivery, saying it will only take an afternoon. Before anyone starts work on it, what should happen first, and why might starting straight away cause trouble later?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. A baseline is the approved version of scope, schedule and cost that the project is measured against. A change request is a formal written proposal to alter something in a baseline or in a deliverable. A change control board, often called a CCB, is the group with authority to approve, reject or defer requests; on small work it may be a single sponsor or product owner. An impact analysis estimates what a change does to time, cost, quality, risk and other work before a decision is made. A change log is the register of every request and its outcome.

Why it works: a change that bypasses the process still changes the work, but nobody has checked its cost, and other people keep working from the old plan. Routing every request through one gate keeps the baseline honest.

Worked example. A sponsor asks for an extra report, saying it takes an afternoon. Step 1: the project manager logs it as a change request in the change log, with the requester and date. Step 2: the team's impact analysis finds it needs two days of design, touches the reporting module, and pushes integration testing back by one day. Step 3: the CCB reviews the estimate and the schedule effect and defers the request to the next release. Step 4: the project manager tells the sponsor and team the status, and the change log shows deferred with a reason, not silently dropped.

Common mistake: letting the team quietly absorb the change, so the schedule and the documents still show the old plan.

Consequence: a change made without a record leaves the plan wrong, so later forecasts and status reports mislead everyone who relies on them. Approved changes must be reflected in the schedule, budget, requirements and other plan documents, and the updated baseline shared with stakeholders.

questions.prompt: A hospital's IT team is building a nurse-scheduling tool for a 6-week project. A charge nurse requests a shift-swap feature. Step 1: the project manager logs the request in the change log with the requester's name and the date received. Step 2: the impact analysis estimates 3 days of build and testing, adds load to the rostering module, and moves the go-live date back by 2 days. Step 3: the change control board reviews the estimate and the schedule effect and approves the request. Step 4 is not shown. Which action completes the process?
choices: Update the schedule, budget and requirements documents to match the approved change, then share the updated baseline with stakeholders.
Ask the testers to absorb the 3 added days within their existing buffer so the plan dates stay the same.
Wait until the shift-swap feature is finished before changing any plan document, so the plan reflects what was built.
Keep the original baseline unchanged and report the new go-live date only in the next status meeting.
questions.why: Once a change is approved, the plan documents and baseline must be updated and shared so everyone works from the same current plan.

questions.prompt: What does a change log record?
choices: The current approved scope, schedule and cost figures.
The impact estimates for each change, without the requester's details.
Only the changes that the change control board has approved.
Every change request together with its outcome, such as approved, rejected or deferred.
questions.why: The change log is the register of every request and its outcome, so deferred and rejected requests are kept on record too.

questions.prompt: A library's kiosk project team lead gets a request to add a barcode-printing option that she estimates she can build in an afternoon. She builds it without logging the request or running an impact analysis. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The kiosk vendor will refuse to deliver the hardware on time.
The change control board will automatically reject the feature at the next review.
The baseline is unaffected because the change was small enough to need no record.
The schedule and plan documents keep showing the old plan, so later forecasts and status reports mislead people.
questions.why: An unrecorded change alters the work but not the plan, so anyone relying on the plan is working from wrong information.

questions.prompt: A four-person app team at a bakery chain has a small project in which the product owner is the only person authorised to make change decisions. A developer wants to know who has the authority to approve, reject or defer a change request. Which answer is correct?
choices: The change log, since it records the decisions made about each request.
The change control board, which on small work may be a single product owner or sponsor.
The impact analysis author, since their estimate determines the outcome.
The developer who wrote the request, since they understand the work best.
questions.why: The change control board is the group with authority to approve, reject or defer requests, and on small work that group can be one person.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just been asked to quickly slip in a small change how change control works on this project, and name one limit or tradeoff of routing every change through a formal board.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them that nothing gets built until the request is written down and its impact is estimated. The project manager records it in the change log, the team assesses effects on schedule, cost, quality and risk, and the change control board decides to approve, reject or defer. Only an approved change updates the baseline, and once it does, the schedule, budget and requirements documents are revised and the new baseline is shared with stakeholders. The tradeoff is that the formal board adds delay and overhead, so a tiny change can wait while the team is blocked on it. For that reason I would suggest a lighter path for small, low-risk items, as long as it still gets logged and its status is communicated, so the record stays accurate.
rubricPoints: Every request is logged and assessed for impact before any decision or work starts.
A named authority (such as a CCB or sponsor) approves, rejects or defers the change.
Only approved changes update the baseline and the affected plan documents.
Stakeholders are told the status, and the cost of the process, such as delay, is named as a tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether a change is approved, deferred or rejected in a messy scenario is best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style situation rather than by a read-only fact list.

lessons.plain: An impediment is anything that blocks your team from moving forward, such as a missing approval, a broken tool, or a decision nobody will make. An issue is a problem that has already happened and is affecting the work right now. Managing issues means working out how much damage it causes, deciding which problem to tackle first, and choosing a way to fix or contain it. A risk is different: it is something that might happen. When that uncertain event actually occurs, the risk has become an issue, and your response shifts from watching it to acting on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has three blockers: a software vendor has not replied for two weeks, a shared test server is down today, and a teammate is unsure which minor naming convention to use. Which one should you act on first, and why?
lessons.teach:
An impediment is a blocker that stops work from moving. An issue is a blocker that has already happened and is causing measurable effect. Impact is how much the blocker hurts the work, measured in lost days, blocked people, cost, or delayed scope. Priority is the order you tackle things in, which should follow impact and urgency together. An intervention is the specific action you take: resolve it yourself, delegate it, escalate it to a sponsor or manager, or monitor it until a trigger date. An escalation threshold is a pre-agreed limit, such as no answer within five working days, that tells you when to move a problem up.

Why it works: a blocker that stops many people today outweighs a vague one that matters next month, and an intervention chosen to match the impact avoids both wasted effort and late surprises.

Worked example: the test server is down, blocking four people with a Friday delivery. Impact is high and urgent, so you restore it or call the infrastructure owner now. The vendor reply is an impediment with a five-day trigger; you set a check date and escalate if the date passes. The naming question is low impact, so you answer it in a short message.

Common mistake: treating whatever is loudest as most urgent, or waiting too long to escalate a risk whose trigger has passed. Once a risk's trigger occurs, it is an issue and needs a named owner and a plan.

In a running schedule, an unescalated vendor delay quietly becomes a missed release, so the trigger date is what protects the deadline.

questions.prompt: A construction crew is idle because a city permit for a concrete pour is still pending. Worked so far: (1) Impact: six crew members are idle each day, and the Thursday pour slips if nothing changes, so impact is high and urgent. (2) Intervention: you phone the permit office contact yourself today, which is a resolve-it-yourself action. (3) The permit reply is still outstanding, and this is the one step you must supply: what do you set for it so the delay cannot quietly grow?
choices: Set a two-day check date and escalate to the sponsor if no answer by then.
Reassign the crew to another site and remove the permit from the tracker.
Treat the reply as closed because you already phoned the office once.
Log the permit as a risk and wait until the pour date to see whether it arrives.
questions.why: A pending reply is an impediment that needs a trigger date and a pre-agreed escalation threshold so that you move it up in time if the date passes without an answer.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes an impediment from an issue?
choices: An issue is any blocker still unresolved, while an impediment is one already costing money.
An impediment is a blocker that has not yet caused measurable effect, while an issue is one that already has.
They are the same thing, differing only in which team reports them.
An impediment is always low impact, while an issue is always high impact.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an impediment as a blocker that stops work and an issue as a blocker that has already happened and is causing measurable effect.

questions.prompt: A bank's migration project has three open blockers. A: one analyst cannot get database access, which was raised first but affects only that analyst's tasks and not the deadline. B: a vendor credit dispute delays cost recovery by about a month but does not stop any current work. C: a payment gateway outage blocks twelve testers, and the test deadline is tomorrow. Which should you tackle first, and why?
choices: C, because it blocks twelve people with a deadline tomorrow, so its impact and urgency are both highest.
A, because it was raised first and the order of raising should decide priority.
All three equally, in the order they appear in the tracker.
B, because the dispute has the largest dollar figure attached to it.
questions.why: Priority should follow impact and urgency together, and C combines the most blocked people with the nearest deadline, while the teaching text warns against treating age or noise as the deciding factor.

questions.prompt: A team logged the risk supplier shipment may arrive late, with the trigger set as no shipment confirmation by 1 March. On 4 March there is still no confirmation, and the project manager records it as a risk and waits for the next status meeting. What is the failure in this case?
choices: It should be tracked as an impediment only after the supplier apologises.
The trigger has passed, so it is now an issue and needs a named owner and a plan immediately, not at the next meeting.
Nothing is wrong, because risks stay risks until they are formally closed.
It is still only a risk, because no shipment has yet been declared late.
questions.why: Once a risk's trigger occurs it becomes an issue, and the teaching text names waiting too long after a passed trigger as the common mistake that lets a delay quietly become a missed deadline.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide whether a blocker is something you should remove yourself or an issue that must be escalated to the sponsor, and name one limit of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by writing each blocker down with an owner and an estimate of impact: how many people it stops, how many days it delays the schedule, and whether it touches scope or cost. I rank by that impact first, then by how soon it bites. If I can clear it within my authority and within the day, I do it myself. If it needs a decision or resource I cannot commit, I escalate, and I check the escalation threshold we agreed earlier. A limit of this approach is that my impact estimates are only as good as the information I have, so a blocker that looks minor can hide a dependency I have not mapped. That is why I re-check the estimate at each status meeting and treat any risk whose trigger date has passed as an issue.
rubricPoints: Defines impediment versus issue and explains that a risk becomes an issue when its trigger occurs
Describes assessing impact on people, schedule, cost, or scope before choosing a response
Explains prioritizing by impact and urgency together, not by who complains loudest
Names specific interventions such as resolve, delegate, escalate, or monitor with a date
States a real limit, such as incomplete information or hidden dependencies, and how to handle it

suggested.rationale: Choosing which blocker to act on and how far to escalate is best learned by reasoning through a mixed-priority situation, which no current mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: Risk management means looking ahead at things that might go wrong on a project, deciding how likely and how damaging each one would be, writing them in one shared list, and acting on the most important ones before they happen. Think of packing for a trip: you list what could go wrong, such as rain or a lost passport, decide which ones matter, and plan for those. On a project, the shared list is called the risk register, and the actions you choose form the risk response plan. Done well, it keeps surprises small and gives the team a calm way to talk about uncertainty.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your project depends on a vendor delivering a component in six weeks. Before anyone tells you more, what would you write down first about that dependency, and which part would you act on now rather than just watch?
lessons.teach:
A risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it happens, has an effect on at least one project goal. The effect can be negative (a threat) or positive (an opportunity). Risk identification is the step of finding candidate risks, using workshops, checklists, lessons from past projects, and conversations with the team. Risk analysis then asks two questions about each risk: how likely is it, and how much would it hurt or help? Qualitative analysis uses rough scales such as low, medium and high. Quantitative analysis puts numbers on it, for example multiplying the probability by the money impact to get an expected value.

The risk register is the single place where risks are recorded. Each entry holds a description, cause, impact, likelihood, owner (the one person accountable for watching that risk), planned response, and status. Keeping everything in one list stops risks living only in people's heads.

Threat responses include avoid, transfer, mitigate and accept. Avoid changes the plan so the risk cannot occur. Transfer moves the consequence to someone else, such as an insurer or a contract clause. Mitigate lowers the likelihood or impact. Accept means you keep the risk and prepare a reserve or fallback.

Worked example: a vendor may deliver late. Step one, the team logs the risk. Step two, analysis rates likelihood as high and impact as two weeks of delay, so it is a top priority. Step three, the response is to mitigate: get a quote from a second supplier now and add a schedule reserve. Step four, an owner and a review date are written into the register.

Common mistake: writing the register once at kickoff and never reviewing it. Risks change, so the register needs regular reviews and updates whenever something new appears.

Consequence: a risk that is not tracked turns into an issue on the day it hits, so the team reacts with no prepared response.

questions.prompt: A regional library network is adding a lending app that stores patron data with an outside hosting vendor. The team logs the risk: the vendor might fail the privacy audit, which would delay launch. Step two, analysis: likelihood is rated medium at about 30 percent, and the impact is a six-week launch slip plus roughly 20,000 in rework, so the expected value is about 6,000. Step three is missing: the team pays for an independent privacy review before signing, which is expected to cut the chance of failing the audit to about 10 percent but does not remove the risk. Step four: one named owner and a review date are written into the register. Which response does the missing step 3 name?
choices: Mitigate by lowering the likelihood of the audit failure
Accept the risk and hold a reserve for rework
Transfer the consequence to the vendor through a contract clause
Avoid the risk by dropping the outside hosting option
questions.why: Paying for a review that lowers the likelihood without eliminating the risk is mitigation, because mitigation reduces likelihood or impact while the risk remains in the register.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a risk in project management?
choices: A task scheduled on the plan with a known start date
An uncertain event or condition that, if it happens, affects at least one project goal
A problem that has already occurred and must be fixed
A cost that is already fixed in the approved budget
questions.why: A risk is defined by uncertainty plus an effect on a goal if it occurs, which rules out fixed costs, scheduled tasks, and problems that have already happened.

questions.prompt: A team writes its risk register once at kickoff and never reviews it. In month four a key supplier goes bankrupt, a risk that was never updated. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The risk turns into an issue the day it hits, and the team reacts with no prepared response
The risk is downgraded to a low priority because it was not reviewed
The risk is transferred to the project sponsor without any action
The register automatically updates itself as the supplier's finances change
questions.why: An untracked risk becomes an issue on the day it occurs, so the team has no prepared response, which is the stated consequence of not maintaining the register.

questions.prompt: A project has a risk with a 20 percent probability that a shared test server will fail, and the failure would cost 50,000 in lost time. Using quantitative analysis, what is the expected value of this risk?
questions.why: Expected value is probability multiplied by money impact, so 0.20 times 50,000 equals 10,000.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a risk process how a risk moves from first mention to a tracked response, and name one limit or tradeoff in how we analyze risks.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd tell them a risk starts as a short statement of something uncertain that could affect a goal, such as the vendor being late. We identify it in a session or from past projects, then analyze it: how likely is it, and how much would it cost in time or money? That gives us a priority. We log it in the risk register with an owner, a planned response, and a review date. The response depends on the type: avoid it, transfer it to someone else, reduce it, or accept it with a reserve. The main limit is that likelihood and impact are judgment calls, so two people may rate the same risk differently. Qualitative ratings are fast but coarse. Quantitative numbers are more precise but need data we often lack early on, so I'd start with rough figures and revise them as facts come in.
rubricPoints: Defines a risk as an uncertain event that can help or hurt a goal
Describes identification followed by analysis of likelihood and impact
Explains that the risk register records owner, response and status, and is reviewed
Names a real limit, such as subjective ratings or missing data early in the project

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right response for a scenario with competing risks adds the most, and no listed mission or engine covers project risk registers directly.

lessons.plain: Every project teaches the organization something: what worked, what went wrong, and what took longer than expected. Continuous improvement means capturing those lessons and turning them into changes the next project can use. The organization's shared templates, checklists, standard procedures, and records of past work are called organizational process assets, or OPAs. Lessons learned are the findings a team writes down during and after the work. Updating OPAs means putting those findings into the shared material so they are not lost when people move on. A project manager does this during the project and again at closing, not only once at the end.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team finishes a project, and several members privately know that one step caused a two-week delay, but nothing is written down. Three months later a new team hits the same delay. What is the most likely reason, and what single step could have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
A lessons learned register is a project record that lists each lesson: what happened, its cause, its effect, and what to do differently. Organizational process assets, or OPAs, are everything the organization owns and reuses to run projects. They include process assets such as checklists, templates, policies, and standard procedures, and knowledge assets such as a lessons learned repository and records of past projects. Updating OPAs means revising that shared material so future projects use the improved version. This works because estimates and plans get better when they are based on what really happened before, and the same mistake is avoided by default instead of by memory.

Worked example. Project A lost four weeks in testing because the test environment was requested in week ten. Step 1: the project manager records the lesson in the register: cause, the late request; effect, a four-week delay; recommendation, request test environments at planning. Step 2: at closing, the manager reviews the lesson with the sponsor and the project management office. Step 3: the manager edits the planning checklist, an OPA, to add an environment request at kickoff. Step 4: the lesson is filed in the lessons learned repository. Step 5: Project B uses the updated checklist, requests its environment in week one, and avoids the delay.

Common mistake: writing the lesson down and filing it without changing any OPA, so the next team never sees it. Another mistake is treating lessons as a list of blame. In a running organization, the consequence of skipping the update is that the same delay returns on every new project, even though the answer is already on file.

A lesson is only improvement once the shared process has changed.

questions.prompt: A call-centre software project lost two weeks after go-live because agent training was scheduled after the system launched, so staff handled customers on a tool they had not been taught. Step 1: the project manager records the lesson in the lessons learned register, with the cause (training after go-live), the effect (two weeks of overtime and longer call times), and the recommendation (schedule agent training before go-live). Step 2: at closing, the manager reviews the lesson with the operations director and the project management office. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the next call-centre project starts from the revised onboarding checklist and books agent training before its launch date. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: The onboarding checklist, an organizational process asset, is revised to add agent training before go-live.
The lesson is shared verbally at the next team stand-up meeting.
The lesson is filed in the register and the project is closed, with no further changes.
The operations director signs the lesson and the team agrees to remember it for next time.
questions.why: Step 3 must change the shared process asset (the onboarding checklist), because a lesson only becomes improvement once the shared process has changed, and the next project's Step 4 depends on that revised checklist.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of an organizational process asset (OPA), as defined for this unit?
choices: The current project's weekly status report, which is only used on this one project.
The sponsor's personal calendar showing meetings for the next quarter.
Notes a team member keeps in a private notebook during a daily stand-up.
A planning checklist that the company's projects reuse to set up each new project.
questions.why: An OPA is material the organization owns and reuses across projects, such as a checklist or template, so a shared planning checklist fits while one-off or personal records do not.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's six-month project lost five weeks because a customs permit was requested late. The project manager wrote the lesson in the register and filed it in the repository, but never edited the planning template. The next project requested its permit late too and lost the same time. What is the core failure?
choices: The register should have named the person who requested the permit late, so future teams would avoid them.
Lessons should only be written at the start of a project, not at closing.
Six-month projects are too long to produce useful lessons, so lessons should only be recorded for shorter projects.
The lesson was recorded in the register but the shared process was never changed, so the next team never saw the fix.
questions.why: Writing and filing a lesson without updating an OPA means the improvement never reaches future projects, which is the common mistake this unit describes.

questions.prompt: During a hybrid project for a regional bank, a supplier security audit was not booked until week twelve and added five days of delay. The project manager wants the lesson to prevent a repeat on future projects. Which action best applies the idea of updating organizational process assets?
choices: Keep the lesson in the project manager's personal notes so it is remembered.
Write a memo that names the procurement coordinator responsible for the late booking.
Wait until the next annual audit cycle to decide whether anything needs to change.
Update the procurement template used by future projects to book the supplier security audit at initiation.
questions.why: Updating the shared procurement template changes the process future projects use by default, which is what turns a recorded lesson into real improvement rather than a blame list or a memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to projects why writing down lessons learned is not enough on its own, and what the team must do to make the improvement stick. Name one limit or tradeoff of updating shared process assets.
lessons.modelAnswer: A lessons learned register is useful, but it is a record, not a change. If the lesson stays in that file, the next project team may never read it and will repeat the mistake. To make the improvement stick, we have to update the organizational process assets that teams actually use, such as the planning checklist, the estimating template, or the standard risk list, and add the lesson to the shared repository so it is searchable later.
