The tradeoff is that changing shared assets takes effort and review, and a change that fits one project may not fit others. So we should note which projects the change was tested on and review it with the project management office before we change the standard. If we do not, we either overload the checklist with one-off items or make a change nobody trusts.
rubricPoints: Lessons learned are a record that must be turned into a process change to count as improvement.
OPAs include both process assets such as checklists and templates and knowledge assets such as the lessons repository.
The update should be reviewed by the appropriate governance body before it becomes the standard.
A tradeoff exists: shared changes take effort and may not suit every project, so they need scope and validation.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why a recorded lesson must become a shared process change, which is best practised by talking it through.

lessons.plain: When a project changes how an organization works, the people in it have to change too. A project manager looks at the organization's culture, meaning the usual habits, unwritten rules and attitudes that shape behavior, such as whether people share bad news early or wait for permission. They also judge how much the planned change will disrupt specific groups, what those groups must stop, start or learn, and how ready they are to do it. The result shapes the plan: who needs support, how fast the change can land, and what might quietly stop it from sticking.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company tells its field crews to stop using paper timesheets and enter hours in a new app starting next month. The crews have always been paid from paper sheets that supervisors signed without checking. What is the most likely reason the rollout could look successful on paper yet fail in practice, and what would you want to find out first?
lessons.teach:
Organizational culture is the set of shared, mostly unwritten norms that shape how work actually gets done: how decisions are made, whether people speak up about problems, how much risk is tolerated, and what gets rewarded. Culture shows up in behavior more than in mission statements, so assessing it means looking at what people do, not only what the policy says. Useful evidence includes interviews, short surveys, observing a meeting, reading how past problems were handled, and asking who really makes the call.

Change impact is the effect a planned change has on people, roles, processes, tools, and the project's own scope, schedule, cost and quality. Evaluating it means listing the affected groups, describing what each one will stop, start or do differently, and rating both the size of that shift and each group's readiness. Readiness is a group's willingness and ability to adopt the change. Resistance is pushback, active or passive, that usually signals low readiness.

Why this works: a change that fits the culture tends to spread on its own, while one that clashes needs more sponsorship (visible backing from a senior leader), training and time. The plan has to budget for that difference.

Worked example. A dispatch company replaces signed paper timesheets with a self-service app. Step one, assess culture: supervisors approve everything and rarely check details, so approval is a status symbol rather than a real control. Step two, measure impact: supervisors lose their gatekeeping role, crews gain direct entry, and payroll changes how it checks hours. Step three, rate readiness: supervisors are low, crews are medium. Step four, adjust the plan: add supervisor engagement, a parallel run where paper and app both count, and schedule buffer for adoption before the project closes.

Common mistake: treating the change as only a software deliverable and declaring success when the app goes live. Consequence: crews keep paper as a backup, supervisors re-key entries, and the new system holds wrong data while the project still reports green.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility is replacing paper meter-reading route sheets with handheld devices. Step one, assess culture: meter readers rarely report a suspicious reading because the foreman quietly corrects it, so problems stay hidden. Step two, measure impact: the foreman's job shifts from fixing sheets to reviewing flagged exceptions, and billing receives readings the same day instead of at month end. Step three is not shown. Step four, adjust the plan: run a foreman-led pilot route and keep two weeks of buffer before the project closes. Which step belongs in the blank step three?
choices: Sign off the final budget and scope baseline with the sponsor
Notify customers of the new billing dates so they can prepare
Select the handheld hardware vendor so the devices are fixed before anyone is consulted
Rate each affected group's readiness to adopt the change
questions.why: Step three in this method rates the size of each group's shift and that group's readiness, which is the evidence that justifies the plan adjustments in step four.

questions.prompt: In this course, what does readiness mean when evaluating a change's impact on a group?
choices: A group's willingness and ability to adopt the change
The number of people in the group who will be affected by the change
The amount of schedule slip the change is expected to cause
The number of training hours already scheduled for the group
questions.why: Readiness is defined as a group's willingness and ability to adopt the change, which is separate from how many people are affected or how much time is planned.

questions.prompt: A hospital unit's nurses adopt new protocols only after a respected senior nurse publicly endorses them. The project is moving the unit to electronic medication charting. Which response best fits the culture the project has found?
choices: Release the new charting software on schedule and expect nurses to adopt it through normal workflow
Ask the vendor to add more features so the system is easier to use
Remove the paper charts immediately so there is no fallback option during adoption
Secure visible sponsorship from the senior nurse and budget extra training and time before go-live
questions.why: A culture that depends on visible endorsement clashes with a change that will not spread on its own, so the plan needs sponsorship, training, and time built in.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm rolls out handheld scanners to its warehouse. The project declares success at go-live because the devices work. Three weeks later, pickers still keep handwritten lists and supervisors re-enter the scans by hand. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Pickers were not given enough warning, so the project should have sent more emails
The warehouse supervisors were correct to re-enter scans because the system holds wrong data
The project treated the software going live as the deliverable and skipped assessing culture, impact, and readiness
The scanners were the wrong model, so the project should have bought a different device
questions.why: Declaring success at go-live without assessing how people actually adopt the change leaves the new system holding unreliable data while the project still reports green.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would judge whether a planned change is likely to succeed in one department, and name one limit of your assessment.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by describing that department's culture from evidence rather than assumptions: how decisions get made there, whether people raise problems early, and which managers actually check work versus rubber-stamp it. Then I would list every role whose daily work changes, what each person stops, starts or learns, and rate how ready each group is. I would compare the size of the shift with the readiness, because that gap tells me where to put sponsorship, training and schedule buffer. The limit is that my read is only as good as the interviews and observations behind it. A survey can capture stated attitudes while the real norm shows up in what people do under pressure, so I would recheck the assessment after a pilot and not treat a green status report as proof that people have adopted the change.
rubricPoints: Describes culture using evidence of behavior, such as how decisions and problems are actually handled
Lists the affected groups and what each one must stop, start or learn
Compares the size of the change with each group's readiness to decide where to focus support
Names a real limit of the assessment, such as stated attitudes differing from actual behavior

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style organizational scenario to choose the right culture and impact response adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Projects do not run in a bubble. Laws change, new technology appears, political events shift trade rules, and customers suddenly want something different. Evaluating these outside changes means noticing them early, judging how much they touch what the project is supposed to deliver, and deciding what to do about it. A project manager asks: does this change alter what we are building, the order we build it in, or the rules we must meet? The answer may mean changing the scope or the backlog, or it may mean nothing changes at all. The skill is making that judgment on purpose instead of reacting late.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team is halfway through building a customer portal when a government announces a new rule requiring customer data to be stored inside the country by next year. What is the first thing you should do, and why not just keep building?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. The external business environment is everything outside the project team's control that can still change what the project should deliver: laws and regulations (regulatory), new or retiring technology (technological), political and trade events (geopolitical), and shifts in customer demand or competitor moves (market). Scope is the agreed set of deliverables and the work needed to produce them. The backlog is the ordered list of work items waiting to be done, used in agile ways of working; in predictive projects the same idea appears as the scope baseline, the approved version of scope that changes must go through formal control to alter.

Why it matters: a project was approved against the conditions that existed at approval. When those conditions change, the value of the deliverable or even the legal permission to deliver it may change too. The method is to scan for changes, assess each one by asking which scope items, requirements, or backlog entries it touches, estimate the effect on cost, schedule, and value, and then route any needed change through the change control process rather than editing the plan informally.

Worked example: a privacy regulation passes with an effective date five months away. Step 1: log it in the environment scan with its source and date. Step 2: list the deliverables it touches, here the data storage feature and the account export feature. Step 3: estimate impact: storage must move to in-country servers, which is roughly two sprints of rework. Step 4: raise a change request with the sponsor, showing options and the effect on the delivery date. Step 5: once approved, reorder the backlog so compliance items come first and update the affected documents.

Common mistake: quietly absorbing the change into the backlog as if it were an ordinary story, or ignoring it because it is 'not our department'. Consequence: the team ships a feature that breaks the law on day one, forcing an emergency rollback and possible fines, and the audit trail shows no approval for the change. An outside change must become a formal decision about scope, never a silent edit.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's mobile app team learns that the card-reader SDK vendor will stop security patches for the version the app uses, in four months. Step 1: the team logs the vendor notice in its environment scan with the source and date. Step 2: they list the backlog entries it touches: the card-tap payment story and the receipt-export story. Step 3 is left blank and is the only missing step. Step 4: they raise a change request with the product sponsor, showing options and the effect on the release date. Step 5: once approved, they reorder the backlog and update the affected documents. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Estimate the effect of the upgrade on cost, schedule, and the value of the touched stories so the change request has numbers behind it
Quietly add an upgrade story to the backlog so the sponsor sees it as routine work
Ask the vendor to extend support, and skip assessment because the bank's own risk team already covers it
Wait until the patch deadline, then upgrade the SDK in the next release without estimating anything first
questions.why: Step 3 is the impact estimate, which measures the effect on cost, schedule, and value of the touched items so the sponsor can decide on the change request in Step 4.

questions.prompt: In a predictive project, what is the scope baseline?
choices: A ranked list of work items the team may reorder freely at each sprint review
The sponsor's personal wish list of features, kept separate from the approved plan
A record of every change the team has made informally since the project started
The approved scope version, altered only through formal change control in predictive projects
questions.why: The scope baseline is the approved version of scope, and in predictive projects it can only be changed through formal control, which is the predictive counterpart of a backlog.

questions.prompt: The procurement lead notices a tariff rise on an imported component and edits the scope document to swap suppliers, with no change request raised. What is the main problem?
choices: Tariffs are geopolitical events, so the change should wait for the next phase gate
The scope document now has no approval record, so the sponsor cannot weigh cost or schedule effects and the audit trail is broken
The document is merely out of date, so a formatting fix in the next routine version update is enough
Only a more expensive replacement supplier would need approval, so the edit is acceptable
questions.why: An outside change must become a formal scope decision through change control, and editing the plan informally leaves no approval trail and hides the effect on cost and schedule.

questions.prompt: A competitor launches a free tier, which makes a planned premium-reporting story in an agile team's backlog less valuable. What should the team do first?
choices: Delete the story from the backlog today so the sprint is not wasted
Ask the competitor for a meeting to understand what they will do next
Log the shift in the environment scan, then assess which backlog entries it touches and how their value changes
Keep the story at its current rank and build it, since the plan was already approved
questions.why: The method is to scan for the change, identify the backlog entries it touches, and estimate the effect on value before any change to scope is made through the proper route.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a new external change, such as a new trade tariff that raises hardware costs, should change the project's scope or backlog. Name one limit of your approach or one tradeoff you would have to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first write down the change with its source and effective date, then list which deliverables or backlog items depend on the affected inputs. For the tariff, that means the hardware components in the bill of materials. I would estimate the impact on cost and schedule with the supplier, and check whether the sponsor's business case still holds. If it does not, I would raise a change request through change control instead of silently swapping parts or cutting features. The limit is that the forecast is uncertain: tariffs can change again before we deliver, so I would present options with a trigger point for revisiting rather than a single fixed answer. The tradeoff is speed against certainty: waiting for better information delays the decision, but acting early may lock in a costly choice.
rubricPoints: Identify the external change, its source, and its effective date.
Trace which scope items or backlog entries depend on the affected inputs.
Estimate the impact on cost, schedule, and value before deciding.
Route any scope or priority change through change control and the sponsor.
Name a limit such as forecast uncertainty or the tradeoff between speed and certainty.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where the learner must choose the right response to an outside change is the most useful practice for this judgment-based objective, and no listed mission covers it directly.

scenarios.title: Warehouse system upgrade: vision drift and a stalled team
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional regional freight company with four warehouses. It is running a nine-month project to replace its old warehouse tracking software with a new cloud system. You have just been appointed project manager, which means you are accountable for planning, running and closing the project. The sponsor, Dana Okafor, is the senior executive who funds the project and has the final say on its goals. Two weeks into your term, you notice three things. In a short survey, the sponsor describes the goal as cutting picking errors by half within a year. The development lead, Priya Sandoval, describes it as a clean rebuild that finally lets the company retire the old system. The operations manager, Tomas Reyes, who speaks for daily warehouse users, talks only about keeping shipments moving during cutover. Meanwhile, two senior engineers have stopped speaking in the team chat after a heated argument over whether to rebuild the system or configure an off-the-shelf product, and a warehouse supervisor has told you the team is waiting to be told what to do. Respond to the following:
1. Diagnose why the team's understanding of the project vision differs from the sponsor's, and describe the first step you would take to realign them.
2. Choose a conflict resolution approach for the engineers' argument and state one ground rule that would stop the dispute from recurring.
3. Name the stakeholder category that fits Tomas Reyes, describe how you would tailor your communication to him, and explain how you would check whether he is satisfied.
subParts: Diagnose vision divergence and first realignment step
Conflict resolution approach and a recurrence-preventing ground rule
Stakeholder category, tailored communication, and satisfaction check for Tomas Reyes
modelAnswer: A shared vision is a single, clear statement of what the project is for and what success looks like, which everyone on the project can restate in similar words. When the vision diverges, the root cause is usually how it was passed on, not people being difficult. Here the sponsor stated an outcome (error rate), the development lead heard a technical goal (rebuild), and the operations manager heard a risk goal (no disruption). Each person filled the gap with their own priority because the vision was never written down in one agreed form and was delivered in different meetings. The first step is a short facilitated session with the sponsor, the development lead and the operations manager together, to agree one vision statement with measurable success, for example picking errors reduced by 50 percent within 12 months with no more than one day of shipment disruption at cutover. Then each person restates it in their own words and you check for match. Common mistake: forwarding the sponsor's slide deck to the team and assuming it has been absorbed. Consequence if left alone: the rebuild scope will grow beyond what the error target needs, and the cutover plan will not protect the warehouses.

Conflict is a disagreement between people over goals, methods, resources or roles. Resolution strategy is the agreed way a dispute will be handled, chosen after you have identified its source and context. Common approaches include collaborating (finding an option that meets the core needs of both sides), compromising (each side gives something up), accommodating (one side yields), forcing (one side decides) and avoiding (postponing). Here the source is a disagreement over method, rebuild versus configure, which has become personal because decision authority was never made clear. The context is a real cost and time pressure, and both engineers hold knowledge the cutover needs, so collaborating fits best. Hold a structured decision session with both engineers. List evaluation criteria tied to the agreed vision (error reduction, cutover risk, cost, time), score each option against them, and have the sponsor confirm in advance that the scores will decide the matter. The ground rule is that technical approach decisions are made against the agreed criteria and recorded in a written decision log, and disagreements are raised in the session rather than in the team chat. Common mistake: choosing a winner privately and announcing it, which leaves the other engineer defensive and resentful. Consequence if left unresolved: the quieter engineer may withhold knowledge the cutover depends on, delaying go-live.

A stakeholder is anyone who can affect, or is affected by, the project. Categorizing stakeholders by influence (how much they can shape outcomes) and interest (how much they care) tells you how closely and how often to engage each one. Tomas Reyes has high interest and substantial influence over day-to-day operations, because warehouse staff must work with the new system and he can advise against cutover if it is unsafe. He fits the manage-closely category. Tailor communication to what he needs: concrete operational detail, not the programme-level view. Send a short weekly written update covering cutover dates, shift impacts and open risks, and hold a standing 20-minute review before each milestone. To check satisfaction, ask him after each milestone to rate on a one-to-five scale how well his concerns were addressed, log the rating, and ask him to pass on feedback from the warehouse supervisors. Common mistake: treating him as a recipient of the same sponsor-level summary everyone else gets. Consequence if left unchecked: concerns that surface late can pause cutover, which costs shipments and resets the schedule.

scenarios.title: Dock Booking Rollout at Tallow Creek Logistics
scenarios.scenario: Tallow Creek Logistics is a fictional regional freight company that currently schedules truck arrivals at its warehouse docks with a shared spreadsheet. The company is replacing it with a dock booking system. You have just been appointed project manager. The sponsor, Dana Okafor, wants the system live in nine months. Some needs are clear, such as booking dock slots, checking in carriers at the gate, and producing a daily report. Others are still vague, such as how the system should handle late trucks and split loads. Part of the work will be done by an outside vendor, Harbor Ledger Systems, which will supply a hosted booking platform and build the link to the company's inventory database. Your PMO has asked you to return four items by Friday. 1. Recommend a delivery approach for this project (predictive, meaning the scope and plan are fixed up front; adaptive, meaning work is planned in short cycles with frequent feedback; or hybrid, meaning a mix of both) and name the complexity factors that drove your choice. 2. Break the dock booking deliverable into a work breakdown structure (WBS, a hierarchy that splits the total scope into smaller pieces of work) with at least two levels, and explain how you will get stakeholders to agree that this scope is correct. 3. At month four, the baseline shows planned value (PV, the budgeted value of work scheduled to be done by today) of 50,000 and earned value (EV, the budgeted value of work actually completed) of 42,000. Actual cost (AC, what has really been spent) is 46,000. Calculate schedule variance (SV, EV minus PV) and schedule performance index (SPI, EV divided by PV), and state what you would do about it. 4. Vendor Harbor Ledger has offered either a fixed-price contract (a fixed total price for a defined result) or a time-and-materials contract (payment for hours worked plus costs). Recommend one, give your reasoning, and name one way you would check the vendor's performance during the work.
subParts: Work breakdown structure and scope agreement
Contract type choice and vendor performance check
modelAnswer: A hybrid approach fits best. The warehouse booking rules are well understood, so the core scheduling and check-in work can be planned in advance with fixed milestones, which is predictive. The unclear items, such as late-truck and split-load handling, are uncertain and need stakeholder feedback, so those should be delivered in short adaptive cycles, such as two-week sprints that each end with a working review. The complexity drivers to name are the number of stakeholder groups (dock staff, carriers, finance, inventory), the uncertainty in requirements, the external vendor dependency, and the fixed nine-month deadline. A strong answer ties each driver to the approach choice rather than just listing them.

Build the WBS from the top: dock booking system at level one, then major deliverables such as booking engine, carrier check-in, reporting, and inventory integration at level two, then work packages such as 'late-arrival rule set' or 'split-load booking screen' at level three. Each work package should be small enough to estimate and own. To gain agreement, hold a walkthrough with the sponsor and each stakeholder group, review the WBS and a scope statement that lists what is in and out, record their sign-off or written changes, and file the approved version as the baseline. Simply emailing the document without a recorded approval does not count as agreement.

SV = EV minus PV = 42,000 minus 50,000 = negative 8,000, meaning the project is behind schedule by 8,000 units of planned work value. SPI = EV divided by PV = 42,000 divided by 50,000 = 0.84, meaning about 84 percent of the planned progress has been achieved. A good response also notes that actual cost of 46,000 against EV of 42,000 gives a cost performance index of about 0.91, so spending is also running over. The response should propose specific actions, such as re-sequencing the integration work, adding resources to the critical path, or re-baselining with sponsor approval, and should avoid simply saying 'work harder'.

Recommend a fixed-price contract for the defined booking platform and standard connectors, because the outcome is clear and the vendor carries the cost risk. Where the integration scope is still uncertain, a time-and-materials portion or a capped time-and-materials arrangement may be used for the discovery phase, so the company is not locked into a price for unknown work. A valid performance check is to agree measurable acceptance criteria in advance, such as the share of bookings completed without manual correction in a test cycle, and to review the vendor's delivered results against those criteria at each milestone. Naming a concrete measure is required for full credit.

scenarios.title: Harrow Freight warehouse scheduling project: three pressures in one week
scenarios.scenario:
Harrow Freight Ltd is a fictional regional freight company with about 600 staff and four distribution sites. Its project lead, Dana Ortiz, is running a nine-month project to replace the old warehouse scheduling system with a hosted package from a software vendor. The project uses a hybrid approach: fixed milestones for site hardware and two-week sprints for the software configuration. The project sponsor is Marcus Bell, the Chief Operations Officer. Governance rules set by the company say that any change adding more than 40,000 pounds or more than 10 working days to the schedule must go to the Change Control Board (a standing group of senior leaders who approve or reject changes) before work starts. Project changes at or under that threshold can be approved by the project manager and the sponsor together.

In the same week, three things happen. First, the Northgate site manager asks for a new barcode-scanning feature that the team estimates at 55,000 pounds and 12 working days, and wants it in the next sprint. Second, the vendor's annual security audit report shows that its data-hosting certification lapsed six weeks ago, which the project's risk register had listed as a low-probability risk with the response Accept. Dana must now decide what to do. Third, a national regulator publishes an amendment requiring freight companies to keep shipment records for seven years instead of three, with a compliance deadline eight months away.

Answer each numbered sub-task below.

1. Decide how the Northgate barcode request must be routed, and state what Dana should communicate to the requester and the sponsor.

2. Explain how the lapsed vendor certification should change the risk entry, what action Dana should take now, and how the register and the project's compliance records should be updated.

3. Explain how the new seven-year retention rule should be evaluated for its effect on the project's scope and backlog, and name one piece of organizational documentation that should be updated once the team learns from this week's events.
subParts: Respond to the lapsed vendor certification
modelAnswer: The barcode request is above the threshold: 55,000 pounds exceeds the 40,000-pound limit and 12 working days exceeds the 10-day limit. A threshold is a set value above which a decision must move to a higher authority. So Dana cannot approve it with the sponsor alone, and it must not enter the next sprint yet. The correct route is to submit a formal change request to the Change Control Board, which is the group that reviews and approves or rejects changes that exceed limits. Dana should tell the Northgate site manager, in writing, that the request is logged, what the estimate is, and that it will be reviewed at the next board meeting, with no promise of approval. She should also brief Marcus Bell, because he is the sponsor and must know a change is pending above his authority. A common mistake is to treat the sponsor's agreement as enough, or to let the sprint team start the work quietly to save time. The consequence is that unapproved work can break the fixed hardware milestones and leave the project with an unauthorized scope change that auditors will later question.

A risk is an uncertain event that could affect the project; if it happens, it becomes an issue, meaning a problem that is happening now. The register is the log where risks are recorded with their probability, impact, owner, and response. Accept means the team knows the risk and chooses to do nothing active. The lapsed certification is no longer a low-probability uncertainty: the vendor is already out of compliance, so the risk has become an issue. Dana should recognize this and move it out of the risk list and into the issue log, with Accept no longer valid. Her immediate intervention is to stop any step that sends company customer data to the vendor's hosting environment until the vendor proves current certification, and to ask the vendor for a dated remediation plan. She should also tell the sponsor, because compliance problems are an escalation matter. The register entry should be updated with the date the risk occurred, the new issue status, the owner, and the action taken. The compliance record should show that the requirement was checked, that it failed, and what was done. A common mistake is to leave the item marked as an accepted risk because it looks minor on paper. The consequence is that customer data could sit in a non-certified environment, creating a regulatory and reputational exposure the company thought it had accepted.

The new seven-year rule is a change in the external business environment, meaning a change outside the company's control, such as a new law, a technology shift, a market move, or a geopolitical event. To evaluate it, Dana should first confirm what the rule requires: records kept for seven years instead of three. Then she should trace the effect. The scheduling system must store four more years of shipment data per record, so the data design, storage sizing, archive and retrieval features, and access controls may all change. Each of these becomes a candidate backlog item, and the team should estimate each one. The eight-month deadline gives a fixed date to plan against, and the work should be sized and sequenced before the next milestone, with any scope change routed through the same threshold rule used for the barcode request. Once the team has learned from this week, it should update the organizational process assets, which are the company's reusable templates, checklists, and records of past projects. A useful example is the risk-response and vendor-check procedure, which should now require a current certification check at contract start and at each audit cycle, along with a rule that an expired certification is logged as an issue, not a risk. A common mistake is to treat the regulation as a separate compliance task outside the project, which hides its effect on scope. The consequence is that the team may store records for three years and find out only at audit time that the system fails the new rule.
